title: Better Sound Than I Expected
text:
Most of my experience with Logitech products has been with keyboards and mice, though the company has made products in other segments as well, such as video surveillance systems and Modula-2 compilers. This is the first set of Logitech speakers I have tried and used, and I was expecting them to be a solid mid-range offering. They’ve proven to be better than that.

These speakers are not very large, about as big around as the lid on a container of oatmeal. They’re heavy, though, and in addition to the main speaker they have a bass subwoofer on each. They feel very solid and should hold up under some abuse shy of being dropped on a concrete surface.

My first test was to connect them to my phone via Bluetooth. I plugged them in, turned them on and they immediately started broadcasting their ID. My phone immediately saw them and I was able to pair and connect them without any issue at all. Based on my experience there, the Bluetooth connectivity is excellent. I later tried to connect them to my computer by the audio cable – simple and easy as should be expected.

The main question when using a set of speakers – how do they sound? In a word: excellent. The bass response is solid but not overdriven, the midrange is warm and has good depth, and the highs are sharp and clear without being shrill. I was expecting a more subdued sound profile, but Logitech did a good job with getting these to sound great. I would stop short of calling these audiophile quality, but the large majority of users should be happy.

I bumped up the volume and tried to get these to distort and I was unsuccessful. They remained clear even through the full volume range. I set them in the kitchen, turned up the volume and went to the basement as I was still able to hear the sound clearly – through the ceiling.

I do have speakers that sound better by a little bit, but they cost three times as much and they’re quite a bit larger. Considering the price point and the size of these speakers, these are much better than one could realistically expect.

title: Perfect for on-the-go journaling/blogging ... lightweight and portable, it travels well!
text:
I purchased this to take along on vacations so I could journal (and ultimately blog) about my journeys. The first test was just completed: a 2-week cruise around Alaska (Ketchikan, Endicott Arm, Juneau, Hoonah, Anchorage, Kodiak, Homer, and Sitka). I wanted a full-sized keyboard, portable, and easy to manage that would work with my iPad Pro.

I chose this for the size, the fact that it is powered via my iPad (rather than needing to be charged), and the fact that it's a wired connection via the lightning cable rather than Bluetooth. Nothing against Bluetooth, but not having to deal with pairing simplifies things a lot.

This performed beautifully! Connected easily, and no problems at all with performance. It has some nifty shortcuts, many I didn't use, but at least they're available. Despite being a full-size keyboard, the small size means I can tuck this into my carryon along with other necessities and it doesn't take up much space at all. It's durable, too -- the wire connector appears to be sturdy. I used this a couple of times per day to record events and activities, so it was in and out of my bag often. No problems at all.

It's coming along on my next adventure: a cruise around the North Atlantic (including Greenland, Iceland, and Norway) for 6 weeks.

title: This keyboard is superb, but...
text:
I really wanted to love this keyboard. Having a wireless keyboard to type on a propped up laptop while studying was my solution to really bad back pains. And for the first 2 days I loved this keyboard. The keys don't jiggle when typing, everything about the look/design/feel is sleek and smooth. The integration with my macbook and my iphone was seamless. The keys fought off dust and crumbs for a week.

HOWEVER:

1) Please be wary of the fragility of some of the keys. I had only been using the keyboard for the first day or so when I noticed that my "-" (dash key) was loose. Upon further investigation with a magnifying glass, a small piece of plastic had been broken, which was why I couldn't snap the key back into place. I don't bang keys loudly or carelessly when I typed, and given that I hadn't had the keyboard for very long, I assumed it the product arrived with a defective key. After a few days, I looked at my F2 key (bluetooth key)- I touched this key maybe ONCE while connecting to my iPhone- and found it LOOSE! I can't snap it back into place because of the same broken plastic issue.

2) Logitech does not have/provide spare keys: When I called Logitech to inquire about spare board keys (rather than returning the entire keyboard to Amazon, because I did really love it besides this key popping problem), the customer service representative offered to replace the entire keyboard, which is great, but he also made mention of the fact they they DID NOT MAKE/PROVIDE spare keys for this model. This means that in the future, if just one key becomes problematic, the customer will have to go through the struggles of shipping out the entire keyboard, etc. I confirmed with the customer service representative that they did IN FACT not make spare keys (I was shocked), but perhaps I had spoken with a particularly new/tired/unversed representative.

All that being said, I am awaiting for a replacement from Amazon (I figured the shipping would be faster w/Amazon's superb customer service), and will see whether the new keyboard presents with problematic keys.
Hope the above two caveats help.

title: Good for the price, just wish it had a backlight!
text:
I like this keyboard and I am happy with it for the price. It is comfortable to use, the wrist placement feels good for me. I type all day at work and this keyboard is much better on my upper back than my laptop. The wireless functions have worked well and the mouse is responsive. But there are a few tweaks I would make if I were the product designer, or maybe an upgraded model:

-It's loud. The click clicking of every key is annoying when you listen to it all day and it would be a lot of background noise in something like telemarketing/cubicle environments. The noise is awkward when I am trying to take notes on a conference call.
-The keys have a bit more resistance than I am used to. I wish they were a little more recessed into the keyboard and quieter (like the buttons on most newer laptops)

-It really needs a background light, with dim and bright settings. I work into the evenings and my keyboard is in the ergonomic drawer of my desk. It's perfectly placed for long work hours, but then I tend to go back to laptop so I can see the keys while I work. This is particularly useful when using the 10-key and F functions, as well as the sound controls at the top.
-Similarly, I wish there was a light on the CAPS lock so I can see when I have accidentally pressed it. I find myself defaulting to my laptop for this as well.

title: good Logitech mouse
text:
UPDATE (3/30/2019):

This mouse is still functioning as when it was new. I have replaced my 10-year-old Mac Pro with the 2018 Mac mini. I am still using the original Apple Cinema Display. The Logitech Control Center app was installed so the M705 / Marathon mouse would function properly. From time to time I have to unplug the unifying receiver and reinsert it to regain full access to the mouse and its correct assignments of the buttons.

NOTE: There is a newer version of the M705 mouse that does NOT have the side button (left side next to the thumb). The price I paid was $20 recently, but I have not used the newer version yet since this one that HAS the side button still functions.

ORIGINAL REVIEW (November 13, 2017 ):

This mouse was bought to replace the 4-year-old Logitech Performance Mouse - rechargeable battery - because the mouse acted erratically due to lint and other debris that got into the space between the bottom and the plastic covers over the buttons. It prevented drag-and-drop when it would disconnect while dragging. Sometimes the file being moved ended up in another folder that meant I had to UNDO the move and start over. What a pain.

(I began buying Logitech mouse designs after spending too much - $80 - for the Microsoft M6000 laser mouse that was terrible.)

The duration of the parallel battery design makes it last a longer time - I have not had to replace the original batteries yet, but I have been using this only since March of this year (8 months).

The pointer has a tendency to become up to 5 times larger if I move the mouse quickly back and forth left and right. I don't know if this is the mouse or the computer software. I find this interesting, but it does not concern me so I have not asked if anyone else has had the same experience.

One star has been deducted because the scrolling wheel can be used to move up or down the window I am viewing but the window jumps back to where I started. It does not do this all the time, but when I want to scroll up or down to see what has been displayed, it is a pain to have it jump back down or up to where the page had been.

The weight of the mouse is irrelevant when one uses the mouse. It stays on the mouse pad / surface just fine. I am not sure why someone would object to having a second battery in this mouse. For those who have forgotten any high school physical science, the parallel arrangement maintains the 1.5 volts of a single battery but doubles the capacity / run-time of one battery.

As for the mouse specifications: (height x width x depth): 2.6 x 4.3 x 1.6 in; 70.0 x 109.0 x 40 mm (these are from the Logitech site; I would say these measurements are width x length x height considering the way it usually is positioned). Mouse weight: 4.8 oz; 135 g. Compatible OS: Windows 7, Windows 8, Windows 10, Windows XP, Windows Vista, Mac OS X 10.5 or later, Chrome OS.

For anyone who needs a wireless full-size mouse, I recommend the Logitech M705.

title: OVERPRICED FRUSTRATION:  Difficult to setup, too many unnecesary steps, flawed functionality...another Logitech fail
text:
I've had a love/hate relationship with Harmony for the past 10 years...but no more second chances.

Just like every Harmony I've ever owned, setup for this required a call to tech support. I'm fairly tech savvy, and this should be easy to set up, but it wasn't. And I know it wasn't me because it took tech support 30+ minutes and 7 syncs to make it function "properly". Yes, "properly" is in quotes because even at its best, it was unimpressive.

On my own using the software, syncing failed to load my activities into the remote. And again...it took tech support 7 syncs to make it work.

Even after it was working "properly", it was still frustrating to use:

1) When switching between TV and SMART TV, it would power the speaker bar on and off. Does Logitech not understand that TV and SMART TV are not 2 separate devices and if you are switching from one to the other the sound should be left on? With a remote this expensive I shouldn't have to dig out the speaker bar remote to turn it back on every time I switch activities.

2) Lack of physical buttons for numbers is annoying. Any time I need the number pad I have to swipe to unlock, then swipe to get to the number pad. Technology is supposed to make processes faster...not slower. And yes, I know I can turn off the lock feature...but then every time I grab the remote it does something I don't want, and that something usually requires time-consuming troubleshooting.

3) As I mentioned before, programming this remote is a nightmare (2+ hours) and even then it couldn't stand alone. I ran into problems only tech support could solve, and even then it took 30 minutes AFTER I had all the correct devices loaded. Please note that this was a simple configuration: Sony smart TV/Fios DVR/Samsung speaker bar. All less than 3 years old. After I returned this remote I bought a "learning" remote and endured programming every single button individually, and it still took a fraction of the time.

4) There is no POWER button. Only an OFF button. You turn things on by selecting an activity. And as stated before...switching to a new activity powers things off that a remote this expensive should understand should be left on. If you are going to have a single OFF button that powers down everything with an activity button that turns everything back on, you should have an ON button for each device so you can quickly turn on any device that for whatever reason doesn't turn on when you fire up the system with an ACTIVITY button. And again...having to do an initial swipe to get to the ACTIVITIES just to turn the system on is annoying. Why does Logitech insist on writing code that slows down the power-on process???

5) You cannot utilize the Harmony software without plugging in the device. Why??? When things aren't working correctly (which is often) we should be able to fire up the app just to review the settings. Then, when you do plug the remote in, you have to wait for the remote and your PC to establish communication. Don't software engineers understand that we HATE waiting for technology to do things? Especially when forced to plug in when we don't want to??? Speaking of plugging in, it is difficult with this remote. First off, there is a totally unnecessary door. That door gets in the way when you're trying to plug in, and plugging in is difficult enough already because the mini-USB port is deeply recessed inside the door. Do we really need to cause all this hassle just to hide a mini-USB port? C'mon Logitech...don't you guys own cell phones? Mini-USB doors are annoying and useless (which is why cell phones stopped using them). Try to keep up.

6) Tech support is only good for 90 days. Based on my experience with this remote and 2 previous Harmony remotes, this means that any changes I make to my very simple home entertainment system will not work, and I will not be able to get help to make them work.

A remote that costs well over $100 should assimilate my entertainment system like the Borg. It should be simple to set up, function extremely quickly/efficiently, and be highly intuitive. This device is just another example of technology that steals away hours of your your life that you will never get back.

title: The Usual Logitech Harmony Excellence
text:
What can I say that hasn't been said by 6,200 previous buyers except that this Harmony 650 in silver is a great remote for a small single-remote system.

I'm using it on a patio with a TiVo, a Vizio 40" and an Amazon Basics SB20 sound bar. All three devices were easily found in the Harmony database and entered effortlessly into the remote using the MyHarmony app you download from Logitech to your laptop or desktop computer.

Having used the MyHarmony app to integrate my two Harmony Ultimate hubs for more complex remote IR systems that employ my network/router/phone as interfaces, I was already familiar with how Logitech has set up their software -- so it took only minutes to get the 650 into action.

Hint: before beginning to program your remote, gather the manufacturer and exact model number for each device you are going to control: TV, Amp, Sound Bar, Cable box, DVD player, Blu-ray Player, CD player, whatever. The MyHarmony software will ask you to add all the devices you are going to integrate. You'll need information from as many devices as you have current remotes for. When you're done, you put all the remotes away and use just the 650.

According to the MyHarmony app, the 650 can control 8 devices. I only needed to control three for my patio setup, so it was a simple process.

Bottom line, it's WAY easier to use a single Harmony 650 that to juggle three remotes (TiVo, Sound Bar and TV).

And after just a few minutes of easy online programming that then downloads to the 650 via a USB cable, I'm done.

As the 650 is being used on the patio outdoors, and subject to environmental attack from dust and moisture, I ordered the silicone cover for it. Works great: [[ASIN:B01N2SF2XX Harmony 650 Silicone Case for Logitech Harmony 650 700 Remote Controller Cover Anti Dust Anti-Slip]]

title: Attractive, well made, relatively quiet back lit full, corded keyboard.
text:
This is a very attractive and comfortable keyboard. The keys are fairly responsive (I'd rate them a 7/10 on responsiveness) and have a feel halfway between laptop and regular keyboard. Their noise is diminished when compared to most gaming keyboards but there is still a distinctive soft sound (it's actually quieter than the sound your fingers make if you just lightly drum/tap them on a keyboard without actually typing. Except for the space bar and enter key which are a little louder).

Aesthetics-wise, it is very attractive, the clear plastic edge gives it a nice finished look (though it's of course functionless and breakable, it would protect the keyboard itself and is a seperate molded and attached piece. The lighting is customizable to four settings - off (num lock and caps lock remain on at full brightness at any setting), and then backlights on- low, mid, and high. In general I prefer low lighting and have sensitive eyes and get migraines, and the low setting is pleasant, the higher settings are fine unless you're in the pitch dark and then It's too bright for me. In bright light the top setting is still nice and visible.

The keyboard has all the functions and options like print screen and page up and down and mute/volume controls that I need. I haven't used all of them yet.

The palm/wrist rest is not padded but is comfortable and does have a "soft" feeling coating. It does has sturdy fold out upper feet.

The cord is approximately 71 inches (180 cm).

This is a very slim and comfortable low-profile keyboard that is full size and has great back-lighting options. If it came in multicolor backlighting for a similar price I would've purchased that one as well.

I bought this for a new Lenovo Y910 AIO Win 10 which hasn't arrived yet (thanks UPS for making me wait 3 MORE days now when I paid for 2 day prime shipping), but I tested it on my MSI GE70 laptop running WIn 7 Pro and it was literally plug and play, worked instantly.

The bottom row of keys (ctrl, windows, alt, spacebar, fn, ctrl, are much taller/raised which is a little weird at first (arrow keys and number pad keys match the rest of the low profile keyboard). I may just be noticing it because I have damaged extensor tendons in my dominant left hand which limits how high I can lift 3 of my fingers. Time will tell if I get used to it and stop noticing it.

I've uploaded many photos, one is a composite showing all lighting settings. The differences are much more apparent in person than I could capture on camera.

title: Loving it - with updated, detailed review
text:
September 2018
After months of heavy use, two keys developed a commonly described sticking problem. I switched to my spare till I can set aside project time to dismantle and clean the first one. At this cheap price, it's easy to afford to spare - but it's too bad that you may NEED a spare. Revised my rating to a 4 but still love the remote.

April 2018
I've now switched to Harmony 650 as my main remote.

• Hardware quality and ergonomics: 5
Just feels right in the hand. Lightweight. Buttons are well placed, backlit, feel solid. Screen is well lit, very readable. Sleek. Nicely built.

• Price: 5
Downright cheap for a sophisticated universal remote. Most good ones cost a lot more.

• Software: 4
Very reliable operation, nicely organized features. Learning curve was long (6 sessions so far for individual button programming and teaching of some functions from my old remote). Some features can't be customized, yet there's still lots of flexibility. Complaint: for blu-ray, the Harmony decided each button should control my TV rather than my blu-ray player, so I manually re-programmed every blu-ray button (twice: for "Activities," and for "Device.") Glad a workaround was available.

"Activities" - use this for combined tasks. For instance: my older AV receiver lacks HDMI switching, so I used "Activities" to select the AV receiver's audio input, plus an HDMI selection from an external device I have, plus a TOSlink (optical audio) choice from yet another device. Harmony 650 managed it seamlessly. Now, since most people have an AV receiver with built-in HDMI switching, they won't need my workaround - but this extreme case just proved the advanced feature support is very useful.

Product is so cheap that I bought a spare. The customization software easily pushes an identical copy of my custom programming to a second remote - as a "clone."

Very frequently used buttons (play, pause, reverse, FF, record, stop) are at the bottom, where your hand just naturally holds the remote. (Harmony's more expensive models place those buttons at the top, but I would think you'd need two hands for such models: one to hold the base, one to push those buttons.)

Hope these tips help you shop for your own great remote!

-

July 2017 - First use:
Harmony 650 helped me add a new Roku Ultra player to an older universal remote. (Roku Ultra comes with an RF remote but can accept IR commands from a universal remote.) From the Harmony 650 database, I selected Roku Ultra, then taught its IR commands to my older remote. (Otherwise I would have researched and downloaded each button's discrete codes and pushed through a cable to the old remote.) What a time saver!

title: Good on sale, but you'll want to be gentle with them
text:
These are mostly first impressions. I haven't used the microphone yet, but have used it for mobile games and music.
Got these on Deal of the Day, so I'll base this off that pricing.

Sound is good. Nice lows in game play I hadn't heard before - from the device's speakers (Kindle Fire HD8, ?6th? Gen). Haven't listened to a lot of real music, but they seem like they'll be ok.

They don't fold as flat or thin as I thought they would. Still better than a lot of headsets. Might be good in a laptop bag?

I don't find them that comfortable. The padding on the headband started to give a 'noogie burn' after several minutes. Ear pads were ok. The ear cups were large enough to fit over my largish ears, which was nice.

The durability tho'? Time will tell but there are a couple of things which concern me:
- The cord feels thin and fragile. The cord also isn't replaceable (without disassembly and probably soldering). It didn't seem to fit into the device well. I had to wiggle the plug a bit. May have been gunk in the unsealed connector, but...
- The slides on the headband are metal - which is good. The top of the headband feels like a thin, stiff, brittle plastic - which is not.

Bottom line? If you can find them on sale, they're a good sounding headset, which may last you 'long enough' if you're good to your stuff. If not, the Plantronics Gamecom 818H's (wireless) I also got on sale aren't as good sounding, but have held up to my moderate use for a couple years.

I'd still pick the Klipsch speakers over these for audio quality, but these don't forsake much in the way of audio quality (at lower volumes) for the convenience they add with Bluetooth. The Bluetooth was easy to setup and offers all the range you'd expect. In that vein, these are great for a presenter or trainer, as they can hook up to a PC/Mac and a phone (for music before/after class, etc...

While these are in essence 60w speakers, they don't sound thin, and compared to most soundbars or monitors with integrated sound, they pack quite a punch. In the end they do fall short of some of the old school systems like the Promedias in terms of power or timbre. You cannot go wrong with these, but I'd recommend getting the Klipsches unless you need Bluetooth

You just need to know the names and model numbers of the equipment you want to connect and control. It now controls the Samsung TV, the cable box, AppleTV, and a Blu-ray player. It turns on the TV and connects it to an Amazon fire stick, but does not control Amazon functions (the Amazon fire stick uses a radio frequency rather than IR remote). This is no bother for us, as we rarely use the Amazon unit.

My spouse had become nearly phobic about the multitude of remote controls in the family room, but has taken to the Harmony unit with aplomb. The touchscreen graphical interface is easily used. title: Does not work with Windows 10 Creators Update
text:
Logitech Brio worked fine with Windows 10 and unfortunately stopped working after the Windows 10 Creators Update (1703 Build 15063) Hopefully Logitech will provide a driver soon that supports the newest Windows 10 update.

Update 3/30/2017: Logitech customer care was very helpful with providing help to this issue that worked and I want to share it here. I tried auto-update before but always resulted in an error message. This step actually worked:

To correct the issue:
1. In Device Manager, right-click on BRIO/UNKNOWN device with the yellow exclamation icon, then select Update Software.
2. In the Update dialog select “Let me pick from a list..”, then click Next.
3. Check “Show compatible hardware” (if not checked), and select USB Video Device (not Logitech BRIO) from the list.
4. Click Next.
NOTE: If a list of categories is shown instead, select Imaging Devices, then USB Video Device.

title: Rough start but got it working.
text:
Had a bit of a rough start getting the cam to work properly with my freshly updated Windows 10 machine. However, I did get it working and it's going to do exactly what I need it to do.
1) plug cam in and wait for the windows drivers to load up.
2) Open up the 'camera' app and noticed a really wicked flicker that didn't get better with any settings.
3) download and install the Logitech software that controls the pan and zoom and stuff.
4) Notice no picture at all comes out of the cam anymore.
5) reboot and fiddle with crap that did nothing. Undo the crap and reboot, still in condition above.
6) uninstall the device from 'device manager'
7) reboot
8) plug camera in again and wait for several minutes while Windows figures out what to do.
9) open camera software, everything is perfect.
10) open logitech software, everything is perfect.
11) play with settings, do a test video, everything is perfect.

Also, put the camera on a short tripod and point it straight down to see how it does taking pix of a phone for demos. The auto-focus is focusing in the wrong spot, but when I adjust the manual focus I can get a great picture with the camera about 8 inches off the desktop.

So, I would take off points for not being 'plug and play' exactly, but I was able to get it to work without much fuss. And it's going to be a great camera for my purposes (online testing) and my daughter's (Youtubing).

title: Great for Mac
text:
As someone who has only ever purchased $10 mice over the years, this was a huge leap. Glad I took it!

The button customization is incredible. I'm using a Mac, and there are nearly 20 optional commands for each one. My hidden thumb button goes into Mac gesture mode, which is very handy if you're used to using gestures on a trackpad. The "back" button does a quick zoom, and I set the "forward" button to a regular zoom function which allows me to zoom in and out with the scroll wheel. The thumb wheel I set for horizontal scrolling. The button behind the scroll wheel now allows me to select a portion of the screen for a screenshot.

The intelligent scroll wheel is also brilliant. I didn't think I would use fast scrolling that much, if at all, and it took me a few days to pinpoint the perfect sensitivity, but now I don't think I could live without it.

Tracking is very smooth, and the DPI adjustment is very broad. It's also a great color (I got stone) and very comfortable to use.

title: Really good all around.
text:
Ok so i give these a 3 star, but they are a fantastic headset and I’ll break the dislikes down first and give the likes. THE INCLUDED PHOTO IS WITH MY OWN EAR PADS.

First opening the box, I immediately look for leather ear pads and to no avail there were none, i tryed the headset on and it’s somewhat comfortable but no noise isolation with the mesh ear pads so i changed to the cloth and they were just slightly better on noise isolation but still lacking comfort due to being kind of stiff. I could see the pads that came with this headset being uncomfortable for eyeglasses. So I added my own Leather ear pads and suddenly this became an amazingly comfortable headset.

Next I would like to address the static you get from the detachable cord if you bump it too hard or it rotates while wearing. It’s not often that i get this static but it does happen especially if you do not push it in hard and when disconnecting and reconnecting

Now here are my pros:

The looks of these are so amazing and they feel very sturdy and are comfortable on the head.

Sound is really decent the highs are slightly too high when listening to music to me, but this is a gaming headset so that is actually a plus as it allows you to hear better on FPS type games. Bass is also good they thump pretty hard (not quite as hard as my cloud 2s) and don’t have any distortion at all.

Mic has really good clarity but it does tend to pick up a good bit of background noise and has a slight muffled sound at the end of what you’re saying. All in all very good compared to a lot of other headsets i have used in the past.

I love all of the adapters that this headset comes with it makes it a truly universal headset from every day use on your mobile, to gaming PC/Xbox One/PS4

Also the 7.1 surround is rather good!!!

All in all this is a fantastic all around headset it doesn’t have anything it does outstanding at or completely fails at, it’s simply well rounded. The literal only thing I would change is the ear pads.

title: The best general-purpose trackball is now even better.
text:
This is about the sixth Logitech trackball I've bought, along with half a dozen keyboards, and it's among the best of their products. The M570 has been my favorite pointing device for years, and I've worn out a couple of them -- the L and R button switches take a lot of beating, L especially, and after a couple years the button becomes erratic. This, of course, is a terrible flaw, since it means you may accidentally DROP something that you're dragging across the desktop -- occasionally into some folder you didn't notice -- and then it's a challenge to find the file (or 100 files) you dropped.

Logitech replaces these worn out trackballs for free, unless they last too long, and then I'm stuck buying a replacement. But they last for years, and the M570 is now less than $25, so it's not even $1/month "maintenance" cost.

I mention the M570 reliability mainly because the new MX ERGO is reported to use button switches that are 10X longer-lived, or more. Since that was the only defect in the M570, that should mean the ERGO is pretty close to perfect. If it wears out in 20 years, I probably won't be around to care.

Compared to the M570, the ERGO is heavier and I find it easier to keep in place on my desk. I love the sideways tilt feature, since I can use it lying flat for several hours, and then give my wrist some relief by switching to the more upright position, which allows the side of my hand to rest lightly on the desktop. It's also much easier to relax my fingers without inadvertently clicking L or R.

I suppose if I were using this as a portable controller I might not like the extra weight, and I did often carry the M570 with me on trips. If I were doing that on a daily basis, in a briefcase or backpack, the added ounces and volume (the ERGO is about 20% larger) might be a problem. But the trade-off is that it stays put more easily, on a much larger and tackier rubber base layer, and it's more restful to use.

I do miss the acceleration feature, long a standard among mice and trackballs, but the one-touch Hi-Res button somewhat makes up for it. I would prefer both, and I hope Logitech will reinstate acceleration in the next update of the new configuration utility.

The little nubs that the ball rides on are seemingly indestructible. Some reviewers complain that they're plastic, but I believe they're actually a kind of ceramic or glass. Considering that my oldest M570 (5 years?) still runs smoothly and the little nubs are still round with no visible flat spots, I'd say they're considerably harder than most plastics, and I doubt they are plastic at all. Viewed at 30X they look like ceramic to me -- glossy and absolutely smooth and spherical. In any case, they afford very light, smooth rotation in all directions, and they don't wear out. Like any small mechanism in a hands-on application, they do collect dust and other debris from one's hands, but that accumulation of dust and furch just makes the ball movement gradually increase in friction. Pop out the ball, flick of the little dust donuts with your fingernail, and the thing is super smooth and free-wheeling again.

If I could take off half a star for the lack of acceleration, I might do so, but in all honesty, I've been switching back and forth between an M570 and an ERGO for days now, and I can't say I notice any significant difference in pointer movement. On my 50" UHD monitor, it's a long way from one side to the other, but that's why I use a trackball in the first place -- I can just swipe it a few times at the medium-high speed setting, and I've traversed 3,840 horizontal pixels with barely any effort at all. In the end, if I had to trade the Hi-Res button for acceleration, I'd go with the button, and of course that's what you get with the ERGO.

But all this is really nit-picking. The biggest bonus after comfort is the improved scroll wheel, which now has L and R tilt, in addition to downward clicking, and I've missed that for years using the M570. I do wish it had a few more buttons for less-frequent uses, but there's something to be said for simplicity -- I have a few other pointing devices with lots of buttons, and I was never able to make them indispensable.

The biggest downside is the price. I'm not sure why this costs 4X the price of an M570. Clearly it's more expensive to manufacture, but not by that much, but then it's new, and the development costs haven't been amortized yet. If in a year or so it comes down to $39.95, I'd call it a bargain.

title: Great Harmony control, reliably controls EVERYTHING
text:
TL;DR version: This is a great remote. I go through why you would want to spend this much on a Harmony remote, the specific benefits of this remote over the non-Hub remotes, and what you won't get with this remote (but would if you spring for the much-more-expensive 'Elite' model).

-== WHY HARMONY ==-

Great Harmony control. As a WireCutter.com article on remote controls concluded, if you are in the market for the best remote control out there, for all of the last decade the question could first be narrowed down to "which is the best Harmony remote for me," and this remote absolutely continues the trend. So first, what is great about Harmony over any other remote, and why would you spend more than $100 on a remote instead of picking up an RCA "universal" remote at CVS for $30?

Harmony is not a traditional "remote control replacement" or "universal remote". True, it replaces up to eight remote controls for your entertainment center (and a few more for "smart home" lights and switches if you do those). But it isn't the traditional "switch to the DVD remote, then turn that one; switch to the TV remote, then turn that one on" etc.

Harmony is based around activities, like "Watch a movie" or "Watch TV" or "Play the PS4" etc. When you tell the Harmony to, say, "Watch AppleTV", it makes sure the TV is turned on, the AppleTV is turned on, the HDMI switch is turned on, the TV is set to the correct input, the HDMI switch is set to the correct input, and, importantly, everything else is turned off. When you then hit the "Watch Fire TV Stick" activity, it knows the TV and HDMI switch are already on, that the TV is on the right input, but the HDMI Switch needs to flip to another input and the Fire TV Stick needs to be woken up while the AppleTV is put back to sleep.

This approach means that you don't need to tutor the babysitter on how to use the remotes to turn everything on, or guests, etc. If you want to watch TV, you click the Watch TV button, at which point all the buttons on the remote make sense for watching TV. This decluttering - not just removing seven of eight remotes from your coffee table, but removing the mental model of seven different remote controls you still have to hold in your mind while operating a universal" remote - is the raison d'etre of Harmony, and what has people like myself spending well over $100 for a remote instead of $30 max.

We have had two Harmony remotes in the past - an 880 and then a 650. These came after a multi-year escalation in remote sophistication from the "universal" remote that came with the TV (which couldn't control our AV receiver at the time), to a fancier "universal learning" remote which could be taught the receiver codes, to an even fancier "macro" remote to which we could assign strings of button presses for things like "switch from DVD to DirecTV" and "Turn off DirecTV" etc. The Harmony remotes greatly simplified the workflows we were trying to manage through those macros, and made it so we never hit the "Switch from DVD to DirecTV" macro when we had meant "Switch from CD to DirecTV" macro and got everything out of whack.

-== WHY A HUB-BASED HARMONY REMOTE / THE GOOD ==-

We loved them both dearly, but the main failing with all Harmony remotes is the dreaded state of something - anything - getting out of sync with what the remote thinks is "right". For instance, if Harmony thinks everything is off, but the TV is already on (and, like most TVs, there is a single remote control code to "toggle power" rather than a code to turn it off and another to turn it on), then the sequence of "turn TV on, switch to correct input" simply turns the TV off then sends the series of input-switch commands off to the aether. The 880 and 650 remotes had a handy (if pedantic) "Help" button which you could push in that case, which would go through all the devices for the current activity asking you if they are on (if no, send the signal, ask if it is on now, then if so ask if that fixed the problem), then if they are on the right input, etc. Things would get out of sync if you, for instance, hit the "off" button then set the remote down rather than holding it pointed at all the stuff it was turning off until all the "shut down" messages had been sent, or if someone couldn't find the remote and so dug out the old original remote for the TV and DVD player so they could watch a movie, or if someone was watching TV then left without turning it off and everything went into "sleep" mode and eventually timed out / powered off.

The Companion/Hub is different because it makes such "out of sync" issues much less prevalent. The remote control does not send signals to your equipment, so when you press the "off" button it doesn't matter if you immediately drop the remote behind the couch cushions or hide it behind your back. Instead, all IR signals are sent by the Hub, which is fixed in place (and/or by the IR emitter "bug(s)" if you have a closed cabinet). Since the Hub is mains-powered and fixed in place, it emits a powerful IR beam containing the remote commands, powerful enough to bounce off the people, furniture, and walls of a large room and control your equipment (and, importantly, if it works once it will continue working pretty much always unless three of your walls and all your furniture disappear suddenly).

If someone can't find the remote control, the "emergency" remote is right in their pants/hand: their smartphone. Just load up the "Harmony" app while on the same WiFi network as the Hub is on and you have a fairly well-laid-out "emergency" touch-screen remote control. It isn't ideal (really, a touch screen is a horrible remote control, and that is never going to change), but it allows you to turn things on and control them, with the Hub keeping track of the state. The state of each device (which are on, which input is selected, etc) is stored in the Hub, not in the remote, so each "remote" (physical, smartphone app, etc) can share the same state. In theory, you could buy multiple additional "companion" remotes and everyone on the couch could have "the power" (there are options for pairing new remotes in the software, although I haven't tried that at all).

Finally, while there is nothing to be done technologically about a kid leaving the TV on indefinitely when they leave the room, that remote control app allows us to see if they have done so and turn everything off from the other end of the house.

On the other hand, the Companion remote itself does not have a screen, and so can not usher one through the "did that fix it?" troubleshooting flow-chart. Here again the Harmony Remote app steps in with its "Fix" button. But that's not nearly as convenient as an on-remote button (I'll get to that shortly). Still, with the advances above needing to use this function should go from a once-every-couple-days affair to a barely-ever affair.

The feel of the Companion remote is definitely reminiscent of a high-end well-built gadget (as obviously should be the case given the price tag). The texture is grippy and feels great in hand. The "directional controls" sit perfectly under thumb, with both the activity-switching and (useless to us) smart home buttons out of the way up above, and the (also useless to us since we don't have any numbered-channel-based device in our lineup) numeric pad mostly out of the way below. The "color" buttons are a little hard to get to if you have a device which uses them, but the "playback" controls are just a smidgen below the directional controls and so handy at all times.

The other significant improvement of the Hub over the 880 and 650 (and all non-Hub-based previous remotes) is able to command bluetooth-based devices. This includes Amazon Fire TV Sticks, Playstation 4s (it can not turn the PS4 on, and obviously won't replace a game controller, but can control through all the menus so you can use the perfectly functional Bluray player for movies), and other newer devices. In most it will register itself as a "keyboard" which allows you to control the device as well as use the Harmony phone app to type on a regular keyboard rather than try to use the onscreen keyboard for passwords etc (the PS4 has a horrible keyboard I have found, and being able to use my phone instead would have saved a lot of grief Christmas morning!) It also means that you don't have to switch over to the Fire TV or Apple Remote apps when a password comes up on one of those devices, if you already have the Harmony remote app up.

Between the powerful IR blaster and the bluetooth control, we found that setting the Hub behind (yes, behind) our HDMI switch+Apple TV stack allowed flawless and reliable control of those two, the TV mounted above them on the wall, the Fire TV Stick plugged into the back of the HDMI switch,as well as the PS4 and Wii tucked away behind a cabinet door. We didn't need the IR Blaster bug. If we had, the configuration app allows you to set up which blaster (the hub, the included extension blaster, or a second blaster you can buy online for about $10) controls which devices so you won't have the same signal going out through all the blasters and getting muddled at the receiver. We didn't need that functionality, so I can't say how well it works, but it seems easily configured.

We also don't have any "smart home" "IoT" devices, so I can't comment on the functionality of the Hub to turn lights on/off/dim, control the thermostat, and lock your doors. But there are dedicated buttons on the remote to do all that and the Hub seems to be a fully-functional "hub" for such devices in your home. Look elsewhere for reviews of that functionality though.

-== SETTING IT UP ==-

Setting up is your first experience with the remote, but it is also something you will probably only ever do once. In my case, twice, sort of.

Since we had had a Harmony remote before - the 650 - our setup was immediately available once we logged into our Harmony account (yes you will need an account with Harmony to set this up, although after that you will never have to sign on again). For me, though, it seemed "quirky". For instance, when I turned things off, the HDMI switch would often get left on (and then when turning things "on" again the "power toggle" command would turn it back off instead). So, I cleared out all the old devices (which was more tedious than it should have been), had it re-scan the network (oddly this time it only saw our AppleTV, not the Fire TV Stick, although maybe the Stick had gone into "sleep" mode by then), auto-added the Apple TV it found, then keyed in the model numbers (for this I brought up the old remote's config on my computer and keyed the new config into my phone, much easier than trying to find where each manufacturer secreted away their model numbers on the back panels of their devices). Once the devices had all been added, I started adding activities. It already had all our activities suggested (Watch Apple TV, Watch Fire TV, Play on Playstation, Play on Wii), so clicking on the selection it already had selected which devices it thought should be involved (ex, the TV, the HDMI Switch, and the Apple TV), but had it gotten that guess wrong it is a simple checkbox to add/remove any (the Wii for instance doesn't go through our HDMI switch and instead just to the Component input on the TV, so I unchecked "HDMI Switch" for the Play on Wii activity). Once it knows what is involved, it will ask which inputs each switchable device (the TV, the HDMI Switch, whichever was checked for that activity) should be on - the first activity it also asked to select which input the TV was already on since our TV doesn't have direct control over the inputs but instead runs through the "loop" of inputs - then asks to confirm that all devices had been turned on and set to the correct inputs. Then it had a handy "test configuration" button which would switch the TV input to a different input (the TV / channel selection input), turn everything off, then turn everything on and switch everything to the correct inputs; this is a great feature to make sure everything is working, although we had a few false negatives in there which I'll get to in a moment.

With devices and activities set up, the last thing to do was assign activity buttons on the remote. There are three buttons at the top to switch activities, but each button can accept either a short press or a long press (a second or two), allowing access to six activities. Obviously if you have more than six activities you can use the phone apps to access the others, and if you have fewer than six activities you can double-up button presses so for instance the short and long presses of a particular button do the same thing.

If you have IoT / "smart home" devices this is when you would set those up as well. The six dedicated buttons for smart home stuff can't be repurposed for anything else, so if you, like me, don't have any of that to play with, you can't do anything with those "yellow icon" buttons on the top.

Overall, the summary is that the Companion/Hub pair finally really delivers on the Harmony promise of taking care of all the details and just letting you tell your system what to do.

-== THE BAD ==-

With that start, on to the (few) negatives.

The Companion remote doesn't have to power an IR transmitter. I am assuming that sucked up a lot of energy, since the Companion now gets by with a ubiquitous "coin" battery (CR-2035) as you'd find in a watch rather than two AA batteries, and reportedly lasts the better part of a year before needing to have batteries swapped rather than a month or two. That sounds positive, so here's the downside: I don't think they make rechargeable CR-2035 batteries (a quick google finds a few claims for rechargeable CR-2035s from China, but they definitely aren't as prevalent and cheap as low-discharge AAs). So that fleet of Eneloops (or Amazon Basics) will not help you come time to change the battery. Note that the (much more expensive) "step up" system - the Elite system, or the older Ultimate Hub system - provides a built-in rechargeable battery with charging cradle, so if this is a $220 "failure" you can "fix" it by upgrading to that device instead (based on current pricing, where the Companion is $130 and the Elite is $350).

Along with the battery downsizing went the removal of the largest battery draws in the 650 - the backlit buttons which automatically lit up when the remote was moved about. No acceleration detector here, and no backlit buttons. That said, the remote is so simple and straightforward you should be able to easily use it by feel even in complete darkness.

As mentioned above, there is no screen on the remote. Most importantly that means there is no on-remote guidance or feedback. You can not see which activity you are on (other than, you know, looking at the big TV screen in front of you) without bringing up the Harmony app on your smartphone (which, as mentioned above, stays in sync because all state is in the hub, not in the remotes). It can not provide a "Help" functionality on the remote itself (again, use the phone app for this instead). If you do not remember which of the six activity buttons map to which activity (short and long presses of three buttons with music notes, a TV screen, and a movie play icon over each), the remote can't provide any guidance (although, again, the phone app can give you more descriptive buttons to push there, although figuring out which of the physical buttons would do the same would involve delving into the remote configuration screens). If this bothers you inordinately, the Elite system provides touch access to labeled "activity" buttons and feedback via that screen etc.

We don't have cable and so the "favorites" feature isn't one we have tried out. In truth, I always found that to be a useless gimmick on other remotes when we did have DirecTV - we would remember the channel numbers for our actual "favorite" channels, and assigning a single button to the "107" sequence (or whatever; it's been nine years so I don't remember those channel numbers any more) seemed nice but not overall a great time savings, especially when our TV provider (DirecTV) also provided a similar quick-select channel feature (I forget exactly, but one button press then you had nine channels to choose from which you had declared your "favorites" and pressing the number on the remote or using the arrows to select one would take you there quickly). But, if you do live and die by "favorite" channels, they are here ... just not on the remote itself. You can set them up (but only for the built-in "Watch TV" activity, not for any other activity), but you can only use them when you switch to that "special" activity and bring up the Harmony Remote phone app. Again, the lack of a touchscreen is what kills this feature here; you will find full on-device "favorite channel" support in the Elite model if that is really a deal breaker for you. Otherwise, you'll have to memorize channel codes and enter them like an animal. A quick note on this: all the other "state" of the remote is held in the Hub. Except "favorites". Those get stored per remote / phone app. So your "favorites" can be different from your wife's "favorites" etc. But it also means you can't tell the babysitter to fire up the Harmony app and have the kid-friendly channels all marked as "favorites" for them. They'll have to find those channels themselves.

Also, not a problem for us, but if you have, say, a Roku, Apple TV, Fire TV, Playstation 3, PS 4, XBox, and Wii all connected to your TV, and want to add *ANOTHER* item, you will find you've run out of the eight devices this remote can handle. I would advise buying a remote with room for "one more device", but really, it seems like you would need an absurd setup to blast through the eight supported devices on this remote. If you do, though, the Elite handles up to 15 I believe (I suspect that it also has a different model Hub, since the Hub itself enforces the eight-device limit, not the remote control). This seems like an arbitrary software "up-sell" limitation, but again, the limit is so high on the baseline device that most people won't hit it or care.

A last negative that isn't really a negative at all but inherent in how Harmony remotes work - and why we have an HDMI switch in addition to our TV even though we only have four devices hooked up to the TV. Our TV's "input" control (TCL TV, ugh) is quirky. To switch inputs via the remote, you press the "Input" button which brings a box up saying what the current input is, then "Input" again to switch to the next input, etc. Harmony tries to deal with this situation by having an option for it - basically having one more "Input" press than is needed every time it cycles through the TV inputs. However, if that "input box" is already on screen - as it is when the TV first comes on, or for a minute after switching to a different input - then an extra "input" press will send the TV to the wrong input. From the remote's perspective there is no way to know if that box is showing on the TV when it starts sending 'input' commands. With our Harmony 650 remote, I turned off the "send an extra 'input' button press first" feature and instead just put a "TV Input" button in the same place on all the activity screens. When that became tiresome, we bought an HDMI switch (Monoprice switch, with "CEC" auto-switching turned off) for all the HDMI inputs and so now the TV just stays on HDMI 1 or Component (when we play on the Wii). I still commandeered one of the buttons ("DVR" was unused in all of our activities, and out of the way enough to not get hit accidentally, so became the "input fixer" button) on this remote, saving us from having to deal with the phone app's "fix" feature (or getting up and using the TV's built-in buttons to switch to the correct input).

(Side rant: TV manufacturers need to start putting "Discrete input remote control codes!" as a bullet feature on their boxes, or someone needs to build a site which hooks into, say, Harmony's database so you can easily determine if the TV you are about to buy will be great to use or input-cycling hell for the rest of its days!)

All of these "negatives", with the exception of our TV's "input" mal-design, would be fixed by upgrading to the "Elite" model. It is $220 more, but this is a device you will be holding in your hand every day for years.

-== THE WISHLIST ==-

The only things I see missing in this remote, aside from those mentioned above that are fixed by moving to the Elite model, are:

* A Remote Locator button on the Hub. Come on. This would be SO easy! Never lose the remote, because if you stand up, walk over to the entertainment center, and push a button, it emits a loud chirp sound! Or, do something fancy with bluetooth proximity and the iPhone app. This should definitely be in any remote control with a hub or cradle.

* Make the iPhone app use the volume control buttons to, you know, control volume. This should also be a no-brainer, although it might run afoul of app guidelines. Commandeer the volume up/down buttons to control the volume of the current activity. These are the most-often pressed buttons on the remote, at least in our house, so using the only two physical buttons you can on the phone seems like an obvious "win" for the phone app.

* Integrate with device manufacturer apps, or forge close partnerships. The Harmony remote can do much of what the Apple Remote app can do, but honestly I like the Apple control scheme better, and Siri integration is not available in the Harmony app. Similar issues with Amazon Fire TV and PS4 controls. Not sure if it is doable, but one would think that if the device manufacturer is putting development effort into their own app they would also want their high-end consumers who likely have a remote from Harmony to have a great experience as well.

title: Great Mouse with many Options, once I spent hours figuring out how to get Software to work!
text:
At first I was very excited about this mouse and gave it five stars. It feels Great! However, I began to have problems with my brand new Mini Mac. It would jerk around and not work at times. I tried many times turning my computer off and on and downloading the Installer with all the extra amazing options. It turns out, the installer would not open. After an hour of trying again and again I Googled and found out many people had the same challenge so I called Support. They are sending a new Mouse to handle the Jerking problem as that is a hardware problem and not software since I could not download it.Great customer service, however...they had NO suggestions for the Installer problem. Reading some thought it was a Sierra issue and others a Logitech issue. Without it, all the numerous fancy options are not available!

Today after more time, I FINALLY got it to work trying various methods. I am sharing what worked just in case it might even help One person not have to spend the hours I did to have success!!

Installed Newest Sierra software that came Today 11-14-2017 and tried again after restarting computer. Logitech software still would not install.

Trashed the copies and tried again.
1. Unzipped the file.
2. Dragged blue circle Icon in my Applications Folder myself.
3. Right clicked and asked to Show Contents
4. Opened Resources Folder
5. Double clicked on Box Icon which said Logitech Installer
6. It opened and installed!!! Installed and I Restarted as Requested.
7. When the computer started went into Applications folder
and now there were 2 Logitech Icons, one with the Logitech Options!!! Set up my Mouse!!!
So so Happy!! Hope it helps someone else!

title: Excellent Replacement for MX1100, But Not Without Flaw
text:
I'm a big fan of Logitech mice, and I've been using their products for years. I started out with the MX 1100, which, to my mind, is still the best mouse ever made. This is an excellent replacement for that mouse, and carries over many of its excellent features like a useful dual-mode scroll wheel, good weight, a responsive laser and smooth operation on difficult surfaces like unfinished wood grain.

The first thing I noticed about the mouse was its size. It has a relatively high profile, with a prominent "bump" towards the back of the mouse, so it's good for larger hands. Since it's more aggressively sculpted than many mice, so you might love it or totally hate it, depending on how much you want your mouse to fill your hand.

Definitely superior for palm-grip users, as its cross-section is a little to high for finger grips. The side scroll button is of limited usefulness, and I preferred the orientation on the original MX Revolution, but it's good to see it there anyway. The main scroll wheel has a great smooth feel to it, and it's reluctant to move on its own. The primary fast scrolling mode is great, and the click-scrolling mode is good for gaming. The weight is substantial without being tiring or heavy, and the out-of-the-box sensitivity is decently calibrated.

The back and forward buttons on the side, however, are tiny and easy to misfire. I frequently find myself hitting forward when I mean back, or having to carefully pick between the two buttons with my thumb. And the battery life is not the best, requiring recharging about once a week.

title: Extremely Comfortable Multi-Faceted Mouse …
text:
There is no single mouse that will cover everyone’s personal wants/needs, but the Logitech MX MASTER 2S certainly puts forth a well-designed effort. Aside from a few issues, I found this particular mouse well-suited across the board, including gaming.

WHAT YOU GET

This product is simply packaged with the mouse, charging cable and user guide. The mouse itself is sizable (to a degree) and ergonomically designed for a comfortable hand fit that incorporates the hand’s natural tilt. It has a vertical scroll wheel on the top, a horizontal scroll wheel on the left side, two side buttons on the left (in a unique “yin-yang” position), the standard left/right buttons on top and a vertical scroll function button on the top. The USB charging cord is a USB Micro B and the USB Bluetooth adaptor makes basic use a breeze.

WHAT I LIKE ABOUT THE MX MASTER 2S

- The sculpted design of the mouse is the biggest plus, in my opinion. For occasional mouse use (like my particular work environment), I can adapt to pretty much any mouse, but for sustained use (like gaming), the way the mouse feels is critical. The design of the MX MASTER 2S has long-term use in mind. It is “narrow” in the front for comfortable finger placement and flares out in the back to provide a solid base for the palm. The thumb “cutaway” on the left makes all the difference in that it offers a natural feel with a geometric textured rubber coating that keeps the thumb from sliding. The combination of all these features and the slight tilt allow an open hand to rest naturally on top of the mouse. There is no need to pinch the mouse or angle the hand over it … a completely comfortable and natural fit that allows for more precise and controlled movements with little effort. I definitely notice my hand does not tire no matter how long I use the mouse.

- The mouse functions extremely well on all surfaces. From a couch cushion to the leg of my pants, the mouse performs generally well. Obviously, a better surface is needed for precision, but for general use, a mouse pad isn’t necessary.

- The charge. It only takes a few minutes to charge the mouse and the charge certainly lasts longer than my SteelSeries gaming mouse that is designed for long-term wireless use.

- The software/setup is simple and painless. I’ve owned several Logitech computer accessories and they can all be characterized as being user-friendly and designed using common-sense … the MX MASTER 2S continues this trend.

A FEW ISSUES

- The charging receptacle on the mouse offers a tight fight for the charging cord … a little too tight for my comfort. I need to take a great deal of care to ensure the charging cable is inserted straight into the mouse and take the cable out is difficult. I feel as if it is only a matter of time before the Micro USB B end breaks off in the mouse and would seem impossible to remove without damaging the mouse itself.

- The vertical scroll wheel can be a little finicky at times. Even though there is a smooth scroll lock button, I’ve noticed the wheel will occasionally smooth scroll without the button being engaged.

The ability to customize the mouse functions for up to three computers is a nice, but unnecessary feature (for me). The software interface for it is simple and user-friendly. This is simply not a feature I would find necessary. The biggest value I see in this mouse is the sculpted design, its precision and the super quick/long-lasting charge … these features are the basis for any value I assess to a computer mouse. Aside from the charging cable issue, I love the MX MASTER 2S … the best gaming mouse I’ve used to date.

title: Good but Not Great
text:
I had a Logitech Revolution RX mouse from about ten years ago which was awesome. I would've bought exactly the same mouse if I could have found it, but Logitech doesn't make it anymore. I bought this one instead as it seemed to be about the closest match. Unfortunately, it's not as good.

The mouse is fine as far as overall mousey-ness goes. It's a good size, slightly larger than the chintzy mice that come with most desktops so it fits my hand well. I haven't had any problems with it disconnecting or stuttering, even though the mouse is on one side of my desk and the receiver is in the USB hub on the opposite side of my desk, about four feet away. It has good weight.

That being said, I just don't like using it as much as the older version that it replaced. The scroll wheel is comically touchy. I wish that one notch = one consistent amount of distance scrolled, but that's not the case. If you scroll *very* slowly, you get just a few pixels of scroll. If you move it fast, it zips down the page. But there doesn't seem to be a good middle ground, and no way to adjust the acceleration of the scroll wheel. If you so much as breathe on it while VLC is open, it instantly pegs the volume at maximum, or mutes it. Especially annoying with headphones on; it's a good way to blow out your eardrums. It's probably the least precise scroll wheel I've ever used. Also horizontal scrolling is either on or off (the scroll wheel just rocks side to side as a switch, it's not analogue in that direction), and it's so fast NASA should probably look into using its speed for launching stuff into orbit.

It may be possible to get better performance out of it if I downloaded the Logitech control center, but I've always found it annoying that I need a stub app running in the background to use a mouse properly.

I give it three stars because I use it every day and I only get mildly annoyed with it from time to time. But I can't really justify giving it more than that. It's just not that great.

title: Great when it works
text:
I'm on my 3rd set of this combo, having used this one for 6 months, and while I LOVE the curved keyboard, and the absence of wires on my desk, there are times (like today) when it is completely unuseable.

It's not the batteries. I pulled them out and tested them with one of the highest-rated battery testers available. (ZTS Mini MBT Pulse Load Multi-Battery Tester). They showed 100% capacity.

It's not that the receiver is too far away or blocked. It's on a USB3 hub on my desk, only about 18 inches away.

What's really strange is that sometimes shaking the keyboard seems to loosen up the characters that didn't make it to the computer. (Lost characters are magically "found" after shaking.)

Luckily, this happens rarely enough that it's not normally a problem, but when it happens, there's not much to do but either fight through it or grab another keyboard.

The mouse works better, but still fails to respond from time to time. Not good when trying to select a block of text or making adjustments to a photo.

My earlier versions didn't have so many issues, and I think Logitech has gone too far in trying to save battery life. I'd gladly replace the batteries every month if I had a stable connection.

I expect this to be my last wireless Logitech keyboard & mouse.

title: A general use wireless mouse
text:
The Good
- Uses 2 AA batteries that last up to 2 yrs (not verified)
- Switch to power off/on to save battery life
- Rubber, tacky feel on grip points
- Lightweight, comfortable palm cradle

The Bad
- No printed materials directing you what to do next to setup the thing (yes, I know go to the website and download, but still)
- Middle mouse wheel doesn't glide well. Has a friction like feel to it. Compared to three other mice I have, this feels very odd.
- No ability to choose DPI setting. No idea what DPI this is set at. Feels like 800DPI
- Makes a lot of noise using the wheel
- No integration with Logitech Gaming Software as a device

The Ugly
- Arrived with back pouch opened. Whoever shipped this should have caught this and sent back to Logitech because it was so obvious it was opened. I thought this was where the the small USB dongle was packaged and was about to send back.

Some Stuff To Note
- Out of the box, I installed the small USB dongle into the back of my tower computer. Immediately, I got lags and cursor skips when moving. Had to remove and put the USB dongle in the front header panel to get a clear, unobstructed path. Cursor jumps and lags seem to have went away.
- Without the ability to set the DPI, on a multiple monitor setup, this mouse is less than ideal. If you have to move from monitor #1 to clear across to monitor #4 (I have quad monitors), its a chore at the present DPI setting. I have three mice installed, this one is dedicated to a pen display terminal on another desk. So it isn't a deal breaker. But I wouldn't use this for multiple monitor setups.

title: Good idea, poor ergonomics

Hand movement should have been a top priority to keep the fingers on G4 and the thumbstick as a base reference. Another missing is a little pip on the G4 key so that you don't have to look at it and "feel" where the base reference key is.

The G1, G7, G8, G14, require you to lift your hand. The bottom button below the thumbstick is positioned wrong. It should have been posited to the bottom right corner instead of directly below the stick. Instead, you end up arcing your hand and raising it off the palm pad just to tap the top right of the button not triggering the key.

title: In love
text:
My Logitech Wave served me well for 8 years until it met its end with a cup of tea.

Pros
* Logitech has always been a great brand for me with mice and keyboards
* Programmable F keys. This feature is so understated, and is easily one of my favorite features of the keyboard. More below.
* Media keys don't add any additional bulk to the keyboard
* Wired, so no more batteries. It's also a braided cord, nice touch.
* Keys feel nice (to me at least), I enjoy typing on it, has some tactile feedback but isn't a loud clanking keyboard. It's not silent though.
* Rainbow colored lights! And a button to turn off the lights if needed.

Cons:
* Giant bright G above the escape key and no way to turn off just that light.
* Caps lock, etc. indicator lights are rather large and bright.
* Wrist rest doesn't come off. Not a deal breaker for me, but it'd be nice to have the option.
* LEDs aren't super customizable like other keyboards I looked at, but this one is cheaper. You get what you pay for.

Okay, so about these programmable F keys. You can have your default profile (I have one set to put my computer to sleep). And then you can have a profile for any application. That's right. I do a lot with office products, that have really dumb keyboard "shortcuts" (like alt, j, p, h. how am I to remember that?). I now have the F keys available to do something useful. I haven't yet found a use for them in my gaming (mostly using wasd and the mouse) but I can see the amazing potential here. A little sad that you can't remap useless keys like insert, scroll lock or pause/break

2. Has 4 programmable buttons and 1 programmable wheel.
3. Very smooth operation with thumb.

6. Use the unifying Logitech transceiver so you can connect more than one Logitech compatible devices to it and only use 1 USB port.

CONS:

Overall I am very please with the product and would recommend it to anyone looking for a trackball.

text:
Simply put, this is a fine piece of hardware. After wrestling with the choice of buying a case/cover with a built-in keyboard or buying a detached keyboard, I chose the latter. Then after two months of research and reviews, I chose the Logitech.

It's a bit pricey, but it is worth every penny. It is a great keyboard with wonderful feel. It is back-lit and while I have only used back lighting twice so far, the ability to adjust the brightness has been a benefit.

It feels solid; perhaps because of the aluminum in the face, but more, I'd guess, because it is built like all Logitech hardware.

It connects quickly and stays connected. Even when it sleeps (which is really too quick for my tastes, but I'll accommodate) it reconnects seamlessly.

It works on every app I use, including Notes Plus, the email apps, and all the productivity apps (Pages, Numbers, etc.) that come on the iPad. I've paired it to my iPad and my iPhone and can toggle between them.

I used two other blue tooth keyboards in the past and, even though one cost around $50, it still wasn't suitable for daily work. The Logitech makes my iPad a true business device.

The backlight colors are hard-mapped to five zones, which isn't overly flexible, but the rotating preset looks very smooth, and can fool your brain into thinking each key is rotating colors independently. No dedicated, remappable G-keys, and it's not mechanical, but I use a Logitech gamepad for gaming, so I actually don't miss those features at all.

One detail I especially appreciate is the cable: Good quality sleeved cable, and the USB connector has a keyboard icon molded into it, so when you're at the back of your PC trying to sort out which USB cable goes to which peripheral, you at least know which one is the keyboard. I wish this were more commonly done, as I'm not as good about labeling things as I should be.

title: One Remote to Rule Them All
text:
Although not entirely perfect, the Harmony remote delivers the dream of just having one remote that controls *everything* without having a complicated layout or steep learning curve.

Pros:
-It's RF, so it doesn't matter where you point.
-Button layout covers pretty much everything you'd need in a home theater setup
-Very customizable.
-Every button can actually perform two functions - secondary function activates by long-pressing the button. This is *very* useful.
-Hub is able to learn IR codes from unknown or generic IR remotes (such as LED strips)

Cons:
-Android app is a little clunky. Has to sync to the cloud server *every* time you enter or exit your device menu; interface is not overly intuitive; some options are difficult to find due to unclear menu titles, etc. It works fine once you know your way around, but it's very clunky compared to other Logitech products, like Logitech's gaming mouse and keyboard software for example.
-The button cluster near the top, meant for smart lighting, can only be used for smart home devices. If you don't have any such devices, you evidently cannot use those six buttons for anything. Not even IR LED controllers. As a result, my LED bias lighting is controlled by the Yellow button.
-There's no eject button. Seriously? I mapped my Blu Ray's Eject function to the DVR button, because who needs a DVR anyway? Maybe the "E" button next to the 0 on the number pad is meant to be Eject, but that's kind of a weird place for it. Whatever. It works. It's just a little awkward.

Harmony works on the premise that you probably have four or five remotes, and you probably only use one or two of them at a time, so the buttons on the remote get mapped according to "Activities." For example, if you're watching a live sports broadcast, you don't need your blu-ray remote at the moment, and if you're watching a blu-ray disc, you probably don't need the remote to your cable box at the moment. Also, for most of your remotes most of the time, you probably don't need ALL of the buttons; just the ones you use. So, you setup an activity for watching sports, define which devices in your home theater are involved when you watch sports, choose which buttons you need for those devices, and then map those buttons to the Harmony remote. Repeat the process for Blu-ray viewing and any other activity you want, and Presto! You now have a remote that changes to fit each situation.

It's a little pricey for a universal remote, but then again, it's really not a remote - it's a pretty fully realized control processor for home theaters. If you're just looking for something that'll control a smart tv and a Roku at the same time, this thing is overkill. If you have two or three input devices, plus a receiver and smart tv, this thing is an absolute godsend.

title: An economical, well-designed, easy-to-use keyboard.
text:
I have a lot of Bluetooth keyboards, some dating from the earliest days of such devices.

Until recently, Bluetooth keyboards have been an iffy proposition.

The Logitech Universal Folio, though, is very adaptable, pairs easily and has a very usable keyboard.

I tried it with an Asus ME301T, without doubt the worst 10 inch tablet I have ever owned, a real surprise considering the generally high quality of Asus products.

Logitech has designed a very clever fitting system to hold 9 – 10 inch tablets. You have to make sure the corner clamps are fitted properly, not a huge task.

When you open the keyboard, there are two slots on the keyboard base into which two small projections fit. These hold the tablet securely at a comfortable viewing angle of about 20 degrees from vertical. The keyboard base is wide enough and deep enough to permit comfortably using the tablet while it sits on your legs. That can be a real plus if you’re traveling in a car or on a bus or just sitting on a park bench. In the box instructions are sparse and I haven’t checked the Logitech website. I was able to use the Home, Back, Search, Track and Volume controls without difficulty.

Setup couldn’t be easier. On first use, you have to remove a tab that keeps the two coin-type batteries from making contact. Then just slide the on/off switch to on. There is a key labeled with the Bluetooth symbol. Press it and the scan light starts flashing and pair the keyboard with your tablet. (I had to enter a code from the keyboard.) There are arrow keys, which will be very helpful in text entry and editing.

The keyboard itself is very well designed. The keys have as pretty deep stroke. I initially found the keys to be rather close together, but after a half-hour’s use, my speed was increasing rapidly. There is a palm rest about 1.5 inches wide which is very useful. The top row has dual-purpose function keys: the usual F1 – F12 and specific Android, iOS and Windows functions

The base is fairly heavy, but that insures the unit won’t be sliding all over the place I use.

When you close the unit, there’s an elastic strap to wrap around it to keep it closed.

In more than an hour of intermittent testing, the Bluetooth connection never dropped.

Overall, the Logitech Universal Folio is an easy-to-setup device that connects flawlessly to your tablet and has a very usable keyboard. Logitech claims a 2 year battery life.

This is a very usable and useful unit, priced at a very attractive point.

I obviously like it.

Jerry
