title: Love the Alexa integration AND their Customer Service staff!
text:
Let me start by saying the Customer Service department for ZeroTouch is absolutely incredible! I bought this solely for the ability to access my Amazon Alexa account in the car. I have an Echo and an Echo Dot at home and use them all the time so the Alexa integration was a key selling point for me. I really missed being able to just say, "Alexa, add XYZ to my shopping list" or some other such command while in my car because it always happens that that is when I just think of things such as what I need to buy at the grocery store, etc. There are many other hands free features that ZeroTouch works for as well such as using voice commands for sending text messages or placing calls or navigating home, but the Alexa capabilities set this apart from any other on the market.

I bought the air vent unit and noticed early on that my phone had a tendency to tilt sideways and then fall off while driving. So, not good! My case wasn't particularly thick, but the issue for me is that I use wireless charging for my phone so ZeroTouch recommends placing the metal adapters down at the bottom of the phone so it doesn't interfere with the charging coils and cause overheating. This placement, however, caused my phone to be top-heavy and then tilt and slide around until it fell off the vent mount.

I sent an email to: ZeroTouchHelp@logitech.com and was surprised to receive a response within a little over an hour. We engaged in some back and forth communications going over the problem and exploring solutions. Ultimately, I was sent some additional adapter plates and was able to add additional pill shaped adapters at the bottom, aligned vertically from side to side on my phone. This resulted in sufficient magnetic strength to hold the phone in place and still not interfere with the charging coils.

Now I can use Alexa to my heart's content in the car, all hands free. I can get my news flash briefing, add to my shopping list, check the detailed weather report, send text messages, place calls. ZeroTouch even reads my my incoming texts and emails. I'm a huge fan of this product AND their customer service staff!

title: It does work with Alexa, but the Harmony Android app - so bad words cannot begin to describe its failings
text: I purchased the Harmony Hub to be able to control my media system without using multiple remotes. My setup consists of a Yamaha receiver that controls my media devices and my sound system, which includes a Samsung smart TV and Comcast DVR, along with an Amazon Fire stick, a Samsung Blu-Ray/DVD player, and a Chromecast module. So far I've only used the hub to handle my DVR-receiver-TV set up, which in addition to powering devices requires setting the devices for the right HDMI channels and setting the starting TV channel. Given the amount of effort required to get the Hub to handle that task has discouraged me from seeing if the hub will handle the rest of my system. The problem is the miserable Android software supplied to operate the hub. Logitech should fire whoever devised such an incredibly poor and non-intuitive interface. I'm still messing with getting a setup that will start the selected channel consistently. Editing a setup is as likely to leave you starting over as not, making tuning a setup infuriating. Fortunately, the Amazon Echo Dot capability appears to be solid, since I have been able to get Alexa to consistently activate Hub "activities" that crank up my system (although the TV channel that comes up may not be the one spec'd - I'm still working on that). Working with Alexa is the only reason I'm giving the hub 3 stars rather than 1 or 2 since working with Alexa was the main capability I wanted to have (and if fractional stars were allowed I would go with 2.5). It's hard to tell if the Hub is actually a good product since that Harmony Android app is so erratic, slow, and frustrating, totally unsuitable either as a substitute for a remote or as a means for setting up the hub to operate devices in the first place.

Other than that it was nice and accurate, no mouse pad necessary (though I do use it with a mouse pad most of the time anyway - old habits).

The scroll wheel works nicely and seems to have four extra 'buttons' so to speak. If you push the wheel left or right, as well as a double stage button of some sort if you push down on the scroll wheel. Clicks once, then push a bit more for a second click. I haven't used these buttons much yet but the left and right buttons will navigate forward or backwards on a web page.

The construction of the mouse seems solid. There's no flexing of the plastic anywhere except where there should be, and while I haven't intentionally tested its durability, I have accidentally dropped it multiple times from about 3-4ft off the ground onto concrete, tile, and wooden flooring without any noticeable damage.

Now for the issue:
The only real issue I have had so far is with the pads on the bottom of the mouse. There are three black pads that I assume are to aid in smooth movement of the mouse, but after a few days the pads began to grab my mouse pad and make a scratching noise as it slid across the surface. I attempted to smooth out the pads (which are more like stickers) but ended up just taking them off. They can be removed easily, and peeled off without leaving too much glue residue. No more issues since!

Overall I would recommend this mouse. Its not too small, its accurate, and its durable enough for every day needs. If you rest your palm on the mouse you may want to look elsewhere due to the size of this mouse, and perhaps if you're a more serious gamer you would like something with more bells and whistles but it fits my needs well. 4 stars because the pads I had to remove and occasionally it is slow (10-15 seconds) to connect to my computer when I wake it from sleep, but for the price (cost me 30 not from amazon) its great!

title: Logitech MXR: King of Mice
text:
The Logitech MX Revolution is, hands down, the company's best mouse ever. Superior to even the likes of the Performance MX and the (ugh) MX Master, the MXR, as I like to call it, is a very handy piece of kit for a power user or even a non-professional gamer. It's got some quirks and flaws, but what good design doesn't? I got lucky enough to score two well-cared-for units and trade off between both when it comes charging time.

Pros:
-Fantastic Omron switches on the clicks- these are quality, long-lasting Japanese switches
-Feeling in the hand is amazing
-The scroll wheel is fantastic to use-- far better than the MX Master's
-Generally tracks well (if you get a good one)
-Adaptable to most situations
-User serviceable, if you've got the know-how

Cons:
-Requires a charging cradle to charge up
-Cannot connect with a wire to computer-- must use a dedicated wireless dongle
-Cannot use "Unifying" recievers-- uses dedicated dongle
-Requires software to get the most out of the mouse
-Prices are generally outrageous. Shop around, get a good used one
-Battery life's a bit inconsistent- turn it off at night

All in all, the mouse is amazing. It's not worth $400, but it's a great mouse if you can score a quality used one. Just be careful with the dongle-- Logitech doesn't make or sell replacements anymore.

EDIT 7/1/19: I'm coming back a couple years later to tell y'all how to make the mouse even better. There's a piece of software called "UberOptions" out there-- it's a hacked older version of Logitech's SetPoint software that removes some of the arbitrary restrictions on mouse functionality and adds in a boatload of other options you can assign to your mouse buttons. The only real troubles are that the options can be somewhat confusing and that it won't pick up on the newest Logitech products, which can be a blessing in disguise if you just want the newer product to work unmodified.

title: A Great Addition to any Battle station
text:
I've had a Razer Copperhead, Deathadder, and Logitech G500. This is the best mouse I've owned so far. The Razers were pretty but the finishing wore off after a time, and their customization options were limited. The G500 had great customization but, whether due to logitech or not, the software for customizing DPI stopped saving my settings and thus became annoying. Plus my previous mice were laser, which isn't quite as good as optical.

This mouse has the quick DPI switching I need for playing multiple heroes in Overwatch. Through the software (which works for this mouse just fin) I can set 5 points of DPI scaling as well as report rate. with two buttons on the mouse itself I can cycle between them at will. Every button can be individually programmed however you like, including specific game profiles. There's also an additional 'AIM' button for a quick, temporary, switch to a set DPI (like for sniping.)
The scroll button can toggle between smooth scroll and staggered scroll, which I find useful for browsing and other things.
The ergonomics for my hand is quite nice, the mouse is lightweight but comes with weights you can add to adjust that to your comfort as well.

The braided cable is especially nice, as I hate plastic sheathing which tends to break as often as not.
If you're into lights... it's got those too!

Overall a great purchase for any gamer.

This headset, isnt the worst thing in the world but I don't think I would ever recommend ANYONE buy it.
If you want one, go ahead - but I warn you, it's really really annoying to deal with.

This headset was purchased in April 2017.

The first 2 months I had it, I had absolutely no issues - once the 3rd month rolled around, problems began to arise.

Not only does Amazon/Logitech or even the company you buy protection from provide absolutely ZERO customer support, if you buy the protection plan it's like it's not even worth it because they just tell you to talk to Logitech even if Logitech has told you to talk to them.

Now, after only a few months - I now have to replace the battery, because it no longer keeps a charge. As soon as I unplug the charger, 5 minutes later it starts the beeping process, even though before I unplug it's fully charged. It dies within 10 minutes when it's supposed to have a 12 hour charge.

I don't see the point in having a wireless headset that always has to be plugged in.

If this was like a year old at least, hey maybe i'd get it. But just a few months, really? A dead battery already? I'll replace it, but if the battery doesn't last any longer than 6 months, I'm just going to have to invest in a different headset, because I'm done with this BS.

Don't purchase the protection plan, it's an absolute waste of money. That much I will warn you about. It just turns into a circle of "Talk to Logitech" or "Talk to the other company"

While Amazon's policy is if you bought a protection plan and there's no response within 3 days, we'll replace your item for you - I didn't get a response for 2-3 weeks and it's just been a back and forth battle since. I give up with Support.

title: Does not work reliably with newer Apple laptops without USB ports. UPDATED
text:
UPDATE OCT 2019: This keyboard is no longer viable with newer Mac laptops that don't have a USB port. The dongle does not work properly when plugged into a USB hub. It works sometimes and then will randomly stop working. It will pause for a long period of time, relay only some of the typed letters to the computer, and often switch the order of letters. If I turn off the keyboard, unplug the dongle, replug the dongle, and turn the keyboard back on it will sometimes work for a short period of time before not working again. Logitech told me the dongle is not meant to work properly through a USB hub and that it must be plugged directly into the computer. When I told the rep that the new Macs do not have USB ports, she seemed confused and reiterated that it would not work unless plugged directly into a computer. In the end, Amazon refunded my purchase even though it was past the 30 day return period. I've decided to stop trying to save money and am moving on to the Apple wireless keyboard now.

UPDATE JULY 2019: Here it is two years later. The keyboard I bought in July of 2017 once again has a dead battery. This time I pried open the battery tray and replaced it with a comparable rechargeable batter I found on Amazon. It worked for about a month and now won't function properly. I just purchased ANOTHER one of these. Why? Because I love everything else about it. This time I spent the extra $10 on the extended warranty. It will save me $40 in 18-24 months when I have to replace it again.

I love everything about the use and design of this keyboard. However, I received the keyboard for Christmas in 2014. 13 months later, the battery would not recharge, and there is no way to replace it. I was issued an RMA through Logitech, and they sent me a new keyboard. That was in Feb. of 2016. It is now July of 2017, 17 months later, and the battery is dead again with no way to recharge it or replace it. I have to throw the whole keyboard away and get a new one, which is a waste of materials and money. Logitech - please fix this.

title: How Do I Hate Thee?  Let Me Count the Ways.
text:
Too bad Amazon requires at least one star. If there ever has been a zero star item, it is this product. I was unlucky and didn't start to (try to) work with it until my return window had closed, so I'm stuck with a paperweight. If you're smart, you'll heed this warning (and the many other 1-star reviews) and avoid this piece of, well, you know where I was headed.

First things first, credit where credit’s due: I was approached by Logitech with support when I gave negative feedback. They contacted me by email and responded quickly - and pleasantly - to my messages. Unfortunately, the summary of their responses is “no, it can’t do that; no, that’s impossible; no, that’s not available; no, that won’t work.”

Next, please note that I’m an easy reviewer. I tend to only write a review when I like something, so most of the few reviews I’ve written are 5 stars. Just have your product do what you say it will and I’m happy.

So, this thing: A WiFi-connected IR hub to control up to 8 devices, discoverable by Amazon Echo/Alexa for voice commands. Imagine the possibilities!

Now forget about them. If you’re thinking of buying this because you are tech savvy, you will be sorely disappointed. However, if you just want something to turn on your TV, switch to the Roku input, and turn on your amplifier, this may be for you, as long as you get rid of all your other controls and turn off any HDMI-CEC or any other “linking” technologies. If you don’t, you will find yourself hopelessly out of sync with your hub, with it turning off the things you meant for it to turn on, and vice versa.

The hub by itself only provides “Activities” - as opposed to “macros”. These activities have an “on” and “off” state, neither deletable. Importantly, only one Activity can be on at a time, so if you start an Activity, the hub first turns off the previous Activity. Every Activity tries to power on the devices associated with the Activity, and set their inputs if appropriate. So if you wanted to create an Activity as simple as “Mute TV” (which you could envision telling Alexa when your phone rings), it is likely to 1) Turn off your TV (ending the previous Activity), 2) Turn on your TV (starting this Activity), and finally muting your TV. When you’re ready to unmute, it will likely unmute the TV, and turn off the TV. You’ll need to start another Activity to turn on the TV again.

Whew! Now, there ARE ways around some of this. You can set your TV device to be always powered on, so the hub won’t try to control that (even though “power on” is the first, non-deletable step in EVERY Activity). BUT if you do this, you no longer have access to “Power on/off” commands! Neither “Power on/off” nor “input” commands are available to customize Activities (and neither are any “add-on” commands that you may have trained with your original remote).

I tried both the iOS and the Windows desktop apps to set up the hub. The iOS app froze often and occasionally would lose contact with the hub. It’s not at all intuitive to set up, and here’s an example of lame programming: if you try to add steps to an Activity that involves only ONE device, for EVERY step you add, you must choose the device for that step (and, of course, you have only one choice). Even when I was programming FORTRAN in the 70s, I could have made that choice for you.

You know what I really hate about all this? That it didn’t have to be this way. The hub can send single commands from virtual remotes displayed on your tablet or phone. So clearly they could be strung together in the form of macros. And, that capability *may* be available if you purchased a compatible remote or a remote that includes the hub… there is a “Buttons” function that appears in internet searches. However, it does NOT appear as an option if you have the standalone hub. This was verified by Logitech’s support.

I think many of my objections could be cured with a “macros” function, but the fact that this hub has been out for a few years without it does not bode well for its future inclusion. So, if you were dreaming of having Alexa send a configurable stream of IR commands in response to your voice, well, this device is the nightmare that will keep you up at night.

title: Redemption after a rocky start (first set failed)
text:
Right out of the box:

-Tweeter on the Left-Rear is blown and rattles LOUDLY on anything over 1/6th volume (so any level where you'd want to have speakers at all)
-Main Front-Right channel does not have the same level of sound as the other 4 satellites, and is absurdly quiet.
-Right-Rear has absolutely no sound coming out of it, it's literally not functioning
-Subwoofer is nonfunctional: from 1-4 on bass control there is simply no bass, from 5+ there is just a constant, loud HUM that drowns out the rest of the sound.

Absolute garbage right out of the box. I've been using Logitech products for roughly 15 years now and have never encountered anything from them nearly this crappy. Sub woofer blew as soon as I plugged it in, and it took one of the satellites with it. I was super excited for 150W sound under $150 bucks but I think after this it's time to try another brand :(

UPDATE: After filing for a replacement, I was told that I wouldn't need to send the original back. Amazon had a replacement to me the next MORNING (literally 14 hours after I clicked the refund button).

Now THIS is more like it! now that I have a working set of speakers, I am thoroughly happy for the price. These little guys kick a lot of butt! While they aren't suitable as "party" speakers (if you go past about 1/2 on the volume you get noticeable distortion), these are GREAT speakers for a budget gaming build! I have them set up around me and they do a fine job of handling atmospheric sound (footsteps behind you, babbling brook to your right, slavering zombie to your left, etc...). The subwoofer has a really good amount of kick for its size, and does an adequate job of handling the lows on bass heavy songs (although, again only at "moderate" levels). I like them even more when I force-fill the sound: really impressive range when you go this route, rather than letting it do its native 5.1 mojo.

All in all, after a shakey start, these speakers have won me over. The only reason I don't give them 5 stars is because they dont have screw holes to mount them on the wall like my old Z-503's did.

title: 5 years but finally starting to die.
text:
They were a very decent 5.1 setup for about $65 while they lasted. I have owned mine for 5 years now and have started hearing some idle static and crackling in the volume knob. The static comes in the form of random bursts of loud and quiet hissing while the speakers are turned on. The volume is up but nothing is being played through them. The abnormal sounds comes from all 5 speakers including the subwoofer. Its pretty darn annoying so I think its time to retire them. Before this issue, overall sound clarity regardless of content exceeded the price for sure. As to be expected, the subwoofer will not shake your walls down but will definitely surprise you given its size. It does have an analog volume dial. I find the sweet spot to be at about noon for the best low end warmth without distortion. My only gripe is the weight of the front left, rear left and rear right spks are so lite that if you bump the surface they are sitting on, they will move. So too much volume will also make them move. The front right channel spk contains the power button and volume control and is slightly heavier. Although when you press the power button on the front right spk is slides, which is a bit annoying when you're OCD about keeping your speakers aligned. You end up having to hold the speaker when pressing the power button. In my opinion this should have been fixed with extra weight.

Really good sound quality, good reliability and plenty loud for about $65. For the price I will probably buy another set.

title: Great value for a sturdy mouse!
text:
I've been a Logitech user for decades, so when my beloved MS518 decided to go to that big IT recycling bin in the sky, I was pretty bummed. Since Logitech doesn't make my old model anymore, I decided to mosey into the 21st century and get a wireless mouse. We're all computer geeks in this house, and gamers to boot...but I just didn't want to get a hardcore gaming mouse. I tried them, and it's not for me.

The M705 is a great little mouse for the price. Compact, fits in the hand well, and not so many buttons that you have to spend a bazillion years figuring out how to program them. Uses the same software as other Logitech items and it's very much plug & play. If you're replacing another Logitech, it will import those settings to your new device. Very shallow learning curve to get used to. It uses 2 AAA batteries (included) that supposedly should last for 3 years.

Note that the dongle to plug into your computer is INSIDE the mouse itself, not in the packaging. Took me a few minutes to figure it out and not panic that I was left with a mouse and no wireless transmitter.

If this mouse is built as well as all my other Logitech mice in the past, I'm sure I'll have it for many years to come.

title: It works Okay, but it's a Nightmare to Setup
text:
It's extremely frustrating that the controls may do multiple things to a TV, but wont necessarily sync, which can easily result in a frustrating experience. This is especially difficult to use because you can't have any buttons that do the same thing ALL THE TIME and you cannot program any button functions for when the device is in an "OFF" state.

The remote works by having "states", such as "Watching Tv" or "Playing Games" and all of the buttons on the remote must be programmed under a "state" and when you press the "Off" button then no state is active and only the "State Switch" buttons (the three media type buttons at the top of the remote) have any functionality (that is, to enable the selected "State").

The end result is that if you have a device like speakers or TV that toggles when you shift between activities you can end up with the speakers off and no easy way to activate them via the remote. I really would like to be able to set some buttons to have functions that always have the same functionality no matter what "state" the controller is in.

It gets what I need done, but there's a LOT of wrestling to get it to behave how I want, and there is a lot of frustrating setup. I would only recommend this to die-hard enthusiasts willing to fight for such a comprehensive solution for a multimedia setup, and willing to pay the somewhat steep $80 for the privilege to have that fight.

text:
I am now replacing this set for the second time in four years. This time, I'll be getting something different.

Things I loved about them: the over-ear boxes are comfortable and firm. The stiff mic can be swung out of the way and bent somewhat, but isn't wobbly like some mic wires. The end of the mic lights up when muted and can be easily seen out of the corner of the eye. The sound is fantastic for someone used to $25-40 headphones! And I love being wireless.

But I finally hit my limit with the problems.

Both sets had trouble with the connection to the transmitter. The first headset would randomly disconnect and reconnect a second or two later. The second headset did the same when it was connected to the charger. Both sets got to the point where they would not hold a charge and/or the charging wire would not seat properly into its hole and I would think I was charging it but it wouldn't work (similar to sometimes phone chargers only work if you pull down on them in one direction).

Ultimately each headset's problems increased frequency until they were unbearable - yesterday I was losing connection about five seconds out of every minute (spread out randomly). Very hard to have a conversation when that happens. I just can't justify buying another when I know it's going to fail in two years.

title: Great Performance and Supremely Comfortable
text:
I was pleasantly surprised by the MX Master 2S, both with regards to its comfort and with regards to its functionality.

Comfort-wise I have larger hands, and tend to need to use a claw-grip for most mice. This is fine, but it can sometimes get a little tiring. With the 2S it not only fit my hand great (and the sculpted body was extremely comfortable), but the thumb rest was a great touch a well. I've had mice in the past with thumb rests, and I always like them.

Most of the good mice I have at the moment are gaming mice - high end Logitch gaming mice and a Razer gaming mouse (I also have several cheap mice that are garbage in comparison). These are mice that are around the same price-point of the 2S and so made for a nice comparison. In terms of performance I found all mice of this caliber to be about on par. You do have a slightly stronger connection with the 2S's dongle than bluetooth (which can be noticeable in high intensity game play), but otherwise I was very happy performance wise.

The 2S also did a great job on multiple difficult surfaces I tried out - its usable pretty much anywhere.

The 2S has a nice range of functionality, and I found the thumb-rest button to be a surprisingly nice addition for productivity work. The scroll wheel is classic high end Logitech, which means it has a very different feel than gaming mice scroll wheels (it spins much more easily).

The Flow software works but its a little gimmicky in my opinion, in that its only useful in specific use cases. If you have a situation where you think it would be a legitimate bonus, however, it is certainly a plus.

Finally, battery life has so far been excellent - I haven't had the mouse long enough to wear it out despite several days of use.

As a side note, I was very pleased with how the charging was implemented. The charging port is at the 'tip' of the mouse, so that you can essentially turn the 2S into a corded mouse in terms of how it looks. Its great to be able to charge the mouse while using it, only some other mice I've seen/used.

Overall I'd highly recommend this as a productivity mouse or general purpose mouse. It certainly works as a gaming mouse as well, but if you're only looking for a gaming mouse you might want to consider a corded option. I've found that this mouse also works great for business travel; while the size might seem intimidating it easily slides into place in a bag and its fairly low weight (and it was great having such a full-featured/comfortable mouse at client sites as opposed to the tiny 'travel mice' I've used before).

title: Good budget 2.1 system
text:
Nice little 2.1 system for $35, no issues thus far. I just wanted something small to hookup to my PC if I don't feel like wearing my headphones all day. Took a couple minutes to set up and I was good to go. No issues with drivers when connecting, I'm using an ASUS mobo with Sonic Studio so it immediately detected the system and allowed me to set up the equalizer and some other pre-sets. For $35 this really puts out a good amount of sound and bass, I was really surprised... if you're looking for a cheap, quality 2.1 set up for your PC or TV this is a nice choice. My only complaint would be there are no mounting holes on the back of the L/R speakers, but it wasn't a big deal, just threw some velcro on the back and connected to my wall with no issues.

Almost forgot to mention the wired remote off the sub - that is very nice to have, ran that up behind my PC and attached it to the base of my secondary monitor with a little velcro like my speakers, so it's easily accessible to adjust volume, turn on/off, or plug in headphones - nice little touch.

title: After a month of testing, here are my thoughts.
text:
I was concerned after reading some of the other reviews that this would be a dud, but my experience has been wonderful. I've been using the ZeroTouch for about a month now and I love it. The magnet holds my phone securely while driving (I used the one that fits inside my phone case if that matters--it comes with an inside and outside the case option). It was a little tricky to fit onto my vent, but I appreciate that it stays locked in place. If you were planning on transferring this device between vehicles, that might be a deterrent for you.

The wake gesture also works flawlessly (just hold your palm in front of the phone and then start talking), and set up via the ZeroTouch app took less than 60 seconds. The real draw for me, though, was the Alexa integration. I've grown so accustomed to my Echo Dot at home that I want Alexa everywhere! The one drawback so far is the lack of Amazon Music integration, but I'm hopeful they'll add that. The other thing to be aware of is that using Alexa will use your phone data, so if you don't have an unlimited plan you probably won't want to be listening to audiobooks for example.

Overall, the ZeroTouch does exactly what it claims, and it does it well. I'm really happy with it and I'd be even happier if they offered an iOS version.

title: Works with PS4 and PS VUE with HDMI ARC Port
text: This remote works great to control my Sony 930D, Bose Soundtouch 130, and PS4.  It says in the manual that this remote will not turn on the PS4 or control the PS4 in several apps including Netflix, Amazon Prime, and PlayStation VUE (which is true with the remote in PS4 mode).  However if your TV has an HDMI ARC port there is a goods chance it WILL control the PS4 in these apps on the PS4.  I have the Sony 930D TV connected to the Soundtouch 130 over the HDMI ARC port (hdmi 4), then the PS4 connected to the Soundtouch 130 and I am able to fully control the PS4 including turning it on and off, and throughout the Netflix, Amazon Prime, and PlayStation VUE apps.  Just have to setup the remote to control the TV and it sends commands to the PS4 over the ARC port.  This remote is light years better than the Universal remote for the PS4 and allows you to control all devices with the included remote and Harmony app.  Setup is very easy using the app or you can use a computer as well to set it up.  Love that you can custom program buttons and macros too.  I highly recommend this remote to anyone.  You might need a little tech knowledge to set it up but not much if you follow the instructions.  For those of you out there like me that use the PS4 for streaming and thought you were stuck with the PS universal remote there is hope as long as you have an HDMI ARC port.

title: Tight band, thin wire, awful microphone. Sound was fine.
text:
To preface this, I have used Logitech products for years, and had a cheap $20 headset of theirs for a good five and a half years before it finally began to fail. Abuse on my part, I suspect; I stored it in a place where it could get bumped off of surfaces onto the floor one too many times.

I looked for that model, as it had worked beautifully, been comfortable, and most importantly had not been wireless... but alas, no luck. No longer sold. So I tried this set.

Positives first: the sound was fine. Listening to things, I had no troubles. It's not something I would use if I were nitpicking over precise frequencies, but for chatter on Skype and playing MMOs, no problem. It's USB, so it was pretty much a case of "plug and go" with no finicky troubles over Windows believing it was a real thing. I have had a lot problems with Windows 8/8.1 and wireless Logitech devices, even trying to use powered hubs, so I avoid the wireless headsets these days.

Negatives:
1. The headband was tight, with no real way to loosen it adequately beyond flexing it, and the plastic wasn't strong enough that I felt confident in not-breaking it while doing so.
2. The wire linking the earpiece to the volume control/mute button was TINY. So thin. It was like having a piece of shoelace licorice attached to the thing, very flimsy and weak-feeling, and I don't know about other users, but having an interruption in that wire RIGHT at boob level meant I constantly ended up tugging on it, or bumping it, or accidentally catching it on the edge of the desk with my chest when I went to lean forward. A friend had recommended the model, said the control being mid-wire was okay, but he's a guy. I should have thought about that beforehand. I don't know why they used a good sturdy wire for the part attaching to the computer. That isn't the section of the wire which is going to be yanked on every time somebody turns their head.
3. I could have dealt with all of that if it weren't for the microphone. It was "self-adjusting" and "noise cancelling" -- and it did that very well. It did that SO well that EVERY time I went to use it, I had to loudly start the call going, "La la la la hello I'm saying words, hear my voice you blasted thing and stop -- oh, now you can hear me. Hello, person I was calling," because it cancelled out MY noise... I looked through settings, couldn't find a way to turn that aspect off. No objections with the mic placement, however, and no objections with its behaviour beyond the fact that any time I stopped talking for a few minutes, I had to do a repeat of loudly saying nonsense until it recognised my voice as a voice again, and let the other end hear me.

In terms of my usage patterns, I am on multi-hour calls almost every day. VOIP is one of my primary means of staying in touch with friends scattered across the world. I talk for hours, I play MMOs while talking, or I listen to music on my lonesome. It has been months since I purchased this product, and for most of those months, it has been hanging on a hook as my emergency "if every other headset I own dies" backup, because I dislike using it so much.

The keyboard is large enough, and the keys have enough resistance to them. The mouse scroll wheel is great, with either free flowing scroll, or with the press of the button, "clicky" scrolling. I also like the CD eject button right on the keyboard. The long battery life is also a plus, as is the ability to check battery life on the keyboard and the mouse from the software.

title: USB connector on back eventually goes bad.
text:
As many other people have noted the connector in the back of this is garbage. I went through 4 different USB cables thinking it was the cable that was faulty, but it's actually the connector in the back of the mic. they should have provided a more robust connector, or something to support the cable.

Basically, the retention clips on in the USB-B are too weak and eventually loosen to the point of the cable slipping out, this gets worse over time, every time you have to re-insert the cable it bends the clips more and more to the point where you have to take something tiny and bend them out ( eyeglass screwdriver, tip of a knife, etc). This works for week or so for me. I've had this mic for a little over a year, definitely don't abuse it, it just sits on my desk.

I've had to do this process 3 times now in under 2 months, I'm done messing around with it, I'm getting a new mic from a different brand.

title: Does what it says it does, really slowly. The easiest setup of any remote but the slowest operation also.
text:
After dropping cable, I decided to get this remote to make switching between streaming devices and sources simpler. I'm not sure this product meets that goal. Ten feet from the TV, as my sofa is, seems to be an issue for this remote. It takes several seconds for it to change a TV channel, as it seems to have an incredibly slow sending of each number. For example if you want to tune to 1000, the gap between each number or keypress emulation is substantial enough to be irritating. The same is true for switching between sources and activating other devices.

Setup is as simple as it can be for such a device, I believe - you just enter your model number and it finds the proper codes. This is an excellent feature that worked better than any other universal remote I've owned.

I'm not willing to give up just yet. I will be purchasing the Harmony Home Hub because I've been told that the lag issues I mention in the first paragraph are fixed by adding the Hub, because the Hub does the actual signaling of your devices and the Harmony Remote just sends the Hub your command. Even if that fixes the issue, I still feel that the remote itself deserves no more than 3 stars because it is actually almost as irritating as the problem it solves. Its saving grace is that my mother can watch TV at my house unassisted now, so long as she points the remote at the TV for a good 10 seconds every time she pushes something.

title: Dropping Quality
text:
The latest version of the M525 Logitech mouse is okay but, sadly, it's not as good as the previous version. You can tell the difference because the older, better M525 uses the old style Logitech logo with the crescent and dashes. The newer, worse mouse just has the word 'Logitech' printed on it. The wheel doesn't roll smoothly like the old one but, instead, has a 'gravelly', slightly rough (cheap) feel to it. Likewise, when using the side-scroll, the old mouse was silent where the new one has a loud, obnoxious 'click'. Simply put, the new one has a much cheaper feel to it and, from what some other reviews have said, doesn't last as long as the old one, either.

The bottom line is try and find one of the older M525 mice with the old Logitech logo. The new one will still work, but it simply doesn't have the old, solid Logitech quality feel to it. A real shame.

title: Discontinued?
text:
I'm reasonably certain the M505 has been replaced by the M525, maybe for a couple years now, so I don't know where all the more recent reviews are coming from. You can tell the difference mainly from the sides. The older M505 has a 'swirl' that follows the side contour and the newer M525 has racing stripes (except for the red one which is solid black). There's also a slightly different cover and wheel. The M505 has a small light just above the battery 'hatch' where the new M525 has the light much closer to the wheel, just underneath it.

Otherwise, I suspect they're identical, at least the basic shape. The silver M505 was replaced by a blue M525. It's also worth noting that it looks like Logitech changed their logo and they no longer use the character with the mousepad, mouse, and three dashes but just have a logo with the 'logitech' name.

Because the M505 has been discontinued for some time, I suspect that's why there's a big mark-up for one, at least the places that list on Amazon. You'll have to want one badly since it looks like you're going to pay at least $70, which is pretty damn outrageous when you can find an almost identical M525 regularly on sale for ~$20. Unfortunately, reviews seem to indicate that quality has dropped on the successive series of M5xx Logitech mice. A real pity since it's otherwise a very nice mouse with the side-to-side scrolling a great feature.

title: Okay for the price
text:
This combo consists of a Logitech K330 keyboard and M215 mouse. The keyboard is full-size, while the mouse is the bottom of the line for Logitech mice (even though there's a M185 mouse) with one important distinction: this M215 is unifying.

Unlike all other lower-tier keyboard/mouse combos, with the unifying pieces of this one, if the mouse craps (or you just want a different, better one), it can be replaced by another unifying mouse and still use the keyboard or, conversely, if the keyboard quits, you can use the mouse with a different, unifying keyboard. This is important since the mouse has a somewhat unusual shape with a narrower end which some may not like. Likewise, the keyboard, being full-size, isn't really designed for mobile use.

If that fits your needs, and it can found on the cheap (as of this 10/28/17 update, Office Depot had them on sale for $10), it's not bad, but mainly for the unifying aspect. You can't find an individual, wireless unifying keyboard and mouse for anywhere near that price.

But it should be noted that Logitech has lately been cheapening their products and quality is suffering. You can tell the old, 'good' Logitech products because they have the old style Logitech logo with the word capitalized and the crescent/eye. The new, worse Logitech products simply have the word 'logitech' with no capitalization.

title: Well built, but flawed
text:
I want to like this mouse, but its list of flaws relegate it to just "ok" status.

PROS:
- Well built, and has a good weight to it (I guess if you want it to weigh less, you can run it with only one AA battery, but I really like the weight of it).
- The free scrolling wheel feels good, though many programs do not react well to its use.
- Contours to the hand nicely for many people, I'm sure (more on this in a second).
- Task switching button works like a dream in Windows 10; Windows 7 (which I have at work), not so much.

CONS:
- The mouse is small for my hands, and I don't exactly have big hands. I'm just shy of 6 feet tall, so I'd think I'm pretty average, but this mouse feels like it's about 10% too small to fit my hand, and also not long enough to comfortably fit in my palm.
- Similarly, the scroll wheel is about a half inch too far back for my liking. I want to be able to have the tip of my finger on the wheel, not the middle of my finger.
- The scroll style toggle button protrudes from the top of the mouse WAY too much. It touches my finger constantly and it drives me crazy!
- The scroll wheel clicks left and right too easily. Sometimes, when trying to middle click, the program will register a left/right tilt instead. Very annoying.
- The back/forward buttons on the side aren't contoured like the M510, and I loved that feature on the M510.

VERDICT:
All in all, this is still a solid mouse and it can be found relatively cheap compared to some of Logitech's other offerings. I know that this model has been around for a long time, so it's baffling to me that they have made seemingly zero improvements to this model over the years.

title: Major upgrade over the old Performance Mouse MX
text:
A massive and worthwhile upgrade over the old Performance Mouse MX. The improved scroll wheel is a major benefit, but as a pet owner I especially love the improved laser window that doesn't catch cat hair and require you to dig it out with tweezers. The good: better battery life out of the box, better scroll wheel, debris resistant laser window.

The bad: non-replaceable battery; the original used a standard rechargeable AA which could be replaced with a far superior Eneloop Pro. This one is doomed to slowly losing battery performance with no way to refresh it with a new battery. It also REALLY needs a phone charger; it doesn't last as long when charged from PC.

text: I've had time to use this wireless keyboard for a few months now and I must say it's just been an overall very good user experience. I have mostly been using it to browse through Netflix on a Windows 10 PC I have hooked up to a TV, so I just toggle the power off when I'm watching a show and back on when I need to pause or go back to browsing. There is no noticeable delay at all when you power the keyboard back on, it instantly reconnects with the Unifying Receiver and the trackpad and keys become responsive. The battery life seems very good in my use case and I have had no need to recharge it yet. On that note, I think it's worth paying the extra money to have a rechargeable internal battery and backlit keys, rather than having to use AA batteries as with cheaper Logitech models. The build quality also justifies the cost - this keyboard has a very sturdy feel to it and the keys have satisfying feedback when pressed. I have tested the Bluetooth mode on my PixelXL and it worked really well. I can't see myself using it very much with my phone, but if you are an Android tablet or Microsoft Surface user this would definitely serve as a nice keyboard and mouse for those. title: ... but I have read it may perform a little better in low light
text: I bought this because it was on sale for the same price as the C920 but I had read it may perform a little better in low light.  I like to stream games in lower light so I thought I would give it a try.  The quality is very, very similar to the C920.  In good lighting I would say the quality is identical.  With the proper settings in low lighting the C922 is very slightly better performing but you'd almost have to have the two running side by side to see the difference.  It isn't night and day and isn't worth spending significantly more money on the C922.  For the same price I would say to get the C922 over the C920 due to this alone if not for a very annoying "feature" of the C922 and that is that the camera settings like auto focus, auto light correction, exposure, etc will NOT save.  Every single time you run OBS or restart your computer or run whatever program it is you like to use you will have to adjust your camera settings because they go back to default.  If you have extremely bright, perfect lighting this is OK but for a camera designed for streamers, a lot of whom tend to stream in lower light, this is a deal breaker.  This is not a bug either.  A Logitech representative has confirmed this is by design.  To me this is about the opposite of what you'd want from a "streaming" webcam.  For that issue alone I cannot recommend the C922 over the C920.  I did not test out the 60 FPS capability nor the automatic background removal as I got it primarily for the better low light performance and a very large number of users say those other features are not very well implemented so I didn't really care to test them out.  Due to the settings not saving and the fact Logitech does not see this as a bug which means it will never be "fixed" I will not be keeping the C922 and will continue to use the tried and true C920 for the foreseeable future.

The thing that struck me first was that it feels well-built and actually rather heavy. I would like it to be a bit lighter, but the overall feel of tightness and quality is quite good.

The clicks feel very nice, with a clean crisp sound and feel. The clicks are not loud in my opinion, which is good. The middle click on the wheel is a bit tough to press, so it could be improved there, but it's not bad.

The free scroll wheel is a great feature! It works very well to get to the bottom or top of long web pages or documents. I want this feature on every mouse now. In the standard mode, it works nicely and has a cool, solid feel. The wheel also tilts left and right, which is nice, but I would rather have a softer middle click and lose the tilt.

The overall shape and grip of the mouse is very comfortable for my right hand, but less so for my left. I know someone is thinking, "Obviously, look at the shape...", but I use other asymmetrical mice ambidextrously with a slightly different grip in either hand. I think this mouse's shape could work for either hand, except it's pretty large, so it's just a bit too big for a great left hand grip.

I would recommend that anyone try this mouse, especially right-handers. It feels like it's worth more than its price. I may end up using it regularly at work. I only wish it was a bit lighter and easier to use left-handed.

title: Good ergonomics and excellent value
text:
I really like this mouse. It's quiet. It's accurate. It's comfortable in left and right hands.

The first part of this review focuses on ergonomics:
The left, right, and middle buttons click very quietly. The scroll wheel is also very quiet, if not totally silent like some wheels. The mouse also moves quietly and smoothly on its PTFE feet.

In additional to the mouse clicks being quiet, I like the feel of the clicks. The buttons are pretty sensitive, and I would say they require less effort to press than a typical mouse. Still, I haven't had many problems with accidental double-clicks. I think the button clicks may actually reduce repetitive stress injuries to the fingers because the sharp "snap" clicks of many mice are not present here. The clicking action is much softer, but still provides tactile feedback.

I like the scroll wheel's feel overall. It has easily felt detents, but they are not too notchy. One thing that this mouse gives up is the free scroll feature that some Logitech mice have. That would be nice to have, but it's not a huge loss. If you have to have that feature, you might want to look for a different mouse.

Another ergonomic strong point is the LACK of a tilting scroll wheel. This scroll wheel simply scrolls, and presses down for a middle button click. There's no wheel squirming left and right as you press it down, no accidental left and right scrolls, no straining to keep your finger perfectly centered. It just simply clicks up and down. Beautiful. (Again, if you need the tilt wheel feature, you will have to get some other mouse. I personally think that tilt wheels make mice harder to use in most situations, so I am very glad that Logitech left it out.)

One thing I didn't realize before purchase is that this mouse is also visually quiet. The tracking LED shines outside the visual spectrum, so you can't actually see it in the dark. There's no red glow as most mice have. There is a little green LED on the top that lights when you first switch it on, and then goes off, so it's all dark. So, if you use this in a bedroom, you won't accidentally wake up or blind anyone with the LED if you pick up the mouse. This is a really nice feature! (On the other hand, if you drop the mouse in the dark, you may have a hard time finding it! Consider buying the gray & neon yellow version if think that would be a problem.)

In terms of overall grip ergonomics, I think this mouse is very good. I tend to rest my wrist on the desk and use fingertips to drive the mouse. It's a little on the small side for me, as I have big hands. But I still found it comfortable. I actually use both right and left hands for mousing to reduce repetitive stress injuries. This mouse is not symmetrically designed, and favors right-handers somewhat. But I think it's almost equally comfortable in my left hand. The grip is just slightly different from that side. I would definitely recommend that left-handers give this mouse a try.

The balance of the mouse is rather rear-heavy with the battery toward the back. I didn't find this to be an issue, but if you pick the mouse up a lot, it may be less than ideal.

As far as the mouse sensor goes, I think it's good. I found the sensitivity to be adequate for getting the pointer across 2 large monitors (with pointer speed set at about 80% of maximum on Windows 7). I have found it to be quite accurate for precise graphics work. (If you actually draw with a mouse, or play FPS games competitively, you might find this mouse lacking somewhat. But I think it's great for office work. I didn't do any detailed mousing accuracy tests or anything like that, so this is just based on my everyday experience.) I found that the sensor tracked well on a smooth desktop, a sheet of paper, a pant leg, or the arm of a chair. (I don't like to use a mousepad, so this is good for me.)

Overall, I would say this mouse is excellent! It's very inexpensive on Amazon right now, and I would say it's a bargain. There are many more expensive mice with different features, but I think this mouse does the core mouse things so well that you might not need to buy anything else! With the added benefit of quiet and smooth ergonomics, I look forward to using this mouse for years to come.

title: Techies, steer clear.
text:
I want to stress that this keyboard is perfectly fine for the average computer user. It's easy to set up by following the instructions on Logitech's website. However, if you're an advanced computer user or like a lot of control over your electronic components, you'll run into several problems with this keyboard. The reason I'm giving it two stars is because it lacks certain vital functions that computer keyboards have had for decades, and I will break those down. I bought this due to the multi-device function (nice if you have several desktops) and to reduce the amount of cables on my desk, so I'd say these are the major upsides.

Downside breakdown:
Function Keys 1, 2, and 3: On the K380, these keys (yellow) are used to set up Bluetooth connections with devices. When you want to switch devices, you hit the key that's paired with that device. If you use keyboard shortcuts, these three keys will not function. Even if you do Fn+F1, F2, etc. the keyboard reacts like you're trying to re-pair it with a device. On the other function keys, their OS function comes secondary to the function programmed into the keyboard (e.g. F9 is a pause/play button). This can cause issues if you want to map your keyboard with different functions.

No number pad: Keyboard number pads are a godsend if you use your computer's calculator frequently, or you're required to type mathematical symbols or foreign characters using alt-key codes. You can't do this with the number line.

Bluetooth issues: If your machine doesn't have an onboard Bluetooth receiver, you will have to purchase one separately. It takes several seconds for the keyboard to wake back up after not being used for 30 minutes or longer, so if you jump in and start typing fast right away, the first things you type may get cut off. I've also experienced several Bluetooth failures where the keyboard fails to recognize that the target device is turned on.

Batteries: Not that much of a problem, but generates more physical waste in the form of dead batteries than keyboards that pull power from the machine.

The kicker: There is no option for a USB cable in case of emergency. This keyboard cannot function without a Bluetooth-compatible OS, which means if something systemic goes wrong with your computer or you need to change settings at the hardware level, you won't be able to type in BIOS, nor will you be able to use F keys during the boot sequence. UEFI may or may not have Bluetooth capabilities. This was the biggest problem for me, because it meant having to get a second keyboard to fiddle with boot options.

All in all, it's a decent basic keyboard, but a traditional corded one is more reliable in many computing areas.

title: M720 - A Purported 2-Year Battery Life High Performer, with the Ability to Use with up to 3 Computers
text:
The Logitech M720 Triatholon is a high-performance wireless mouse that can use Bluetooth or the included Logitech Unifying receiver. The mouse can work with up to three computers. It has a very nice scroll wheel that spins effortlessly, and can keep spinning if you remove your finger. The mouse fits my mid-size hand (typically, men's glove size L) perfectly, but it also fits my wife's smaller hand well. It's a very comfortable to hold for long periods. Tracking sensitivity and response is excellent. On the left side of the mouse are three buttons in a row: forward, back, and computer selection (1, 2, 3). The computer selection button, IMHO, is not well-placed. It took me a while to get used to where the "back" button is, as I kept wanting to hit the 1, 2, 3 button. The right and left-click buttons are well placed and easy to operate. The mouse uses a single AA battery, with a reported life of 24 months. The mouse is a little heavy for my taste, but you quickly get used to it. I weighed this mouse with the battery, and it came in at 132 grams (4.65 oz). If you want a mouse for use with multiple computers, this is it! The next model up works on glass surfaces, and this one does not.

Compared with the Logitech M705: The M705 (my previous mouse) weighed in at 111 grams when using only one AA battery (~19% lighter than the M720). With two batteries, I'm guessing the M705 weight would be comparable to the M720. Since I'm only using the mouse with one computer, I'd prefer to have the 1, 2, 3 button removed, or at least in a different, less intrusive place. When using two AAs, the M705 runs for 36 months, and about half that on one. If I really wanted a mouse to use with three computers, I'd want one that works on glass surfaces, as many hotels have glass-topped desks. Too bad Logitech did not combine the 1, 2, 3 feature with the glass compatibility feature!

Overall, I prefer the M705 to the M720, but both are reliable, high-performance mice that stand up to daily continuous use.

UPDATE 12/27/17: This mouse's provided alkaline battery died after just 6 months of use. Not sure if it was a cheap battery, or if the battery life is over-stated for heavy users.

title: Good use-it-anywhere Bluetooth speaker. Good deal as a refurb. At MSRP, I’d skip.
text:
I was amazed the first time I shopped for Bluetooth speakers. The prices seemed totally disconnected from reality. “Mid-range” speakers had price tags in the $100-200 range. At that price, I’m expecting sound like a good quality bookshelf/desktop speaker. What I found wasn’t even close.

This unit, especially at the refurb pricing, is a good deal. The sound quality is comparable to an old-school boom-box, and it’s handled several uses in the shower without any issues. (The downloadable app for a smartphone is useful here; it allows you to adjust the response curve so you can still get room-like sound in the horrible acoustics of a tile shower)

I don’t see myself buying a second one, it’s just something I use occasionally and even if the pairing is as simple and reliable as the maker claims, it’s just a lot of work for something of pretty dubious benefit. If you need two speakers and stereo, wireless is probably more trouble than it’s worth - and reading other reviews here makes me think that’s probably an optimistic take.

TL;DR: Good sound, easy to use, doesn’t mind rough handling, not a big fan of the volume control styling, people think it’s a company logo or something and keep looking around for normal buttons.

title: This thing is legit!
text:
I've had a 'Harmony One' (Now Discontinued) for about 6 years. I was devastated when my one-year-old threw it on my tile and cracked the touch screen display. I wasn't looking forward to paying for the new models which were pushing $200+

Based on my buddy's recommendation, I purchased this Smart Control model with the accompanying 'Smart Hub' and IR blaster for $120. Honestly, I was pretty skeptical, because the remote doesn't look like much out of the box. Turns out, the REAL value is in the Smart Hub. That thing alone makes this a far better remote than my old Harmony One could ever be on its own. This Hub does IR and Blue tooth, so it should cover any of your remote needs.

First thing to understand is that the remote ONLY talks to the Smart Hub, not your individual devices themselves. And it accomplishes this via RF, meaning you don't have to have it pointed directly at the box. And those of you who've had missed commands, especially during start-up and shut-down, know it can be quite annoying to go through the troubleshooting steps to correct it. I've tested this thing from around walls, under pillows and so on. It's solid. The Smart Hub and IR blaster is what's actually talking to your devices. So once you determine you've got them arranged in the best spots, you never have to worry about missed commands again.

Again, the remote looks and feels simple, but I really don't mind any more. This remote comes with a 3V CR2032 nickel-sized battery, so there's no charging or docking station to worry about. I can't say at this time how battery performance is, but I'm hoping the lack of an LCD touch screen will boost performance quite a bit.

You can also completely program your remote via yur phone using the Harmony app. My old remote required use of a pc, which was kind of annoying. And once the remote is programmed, your phone can double as a remote too! It also gives you that added depth of functionaltiy, should you feel the need to get into sub menus.

title: Beware of Blue Microphone
text:
This is an updated review, as my journey with this horrible thing hasn't stopped. When I first bought this in 2017, the mic worked great for 2 weeks. After those 2 weeks, all my audio sounded like I was in a fish bowl. First and second time I had to return it: Amazon was wonderful about replacing the defective mics. Third time, I had to contact the Blue Microphone company themselves, who took 3 months to get back to me. They only replied to my email when I sent a follow up email wondering why there hasn't been a reply. I was finally able to send back the mic directly to the company. After about ten months of intermittently attempting to contact the company to demand a refund, I resorted to reporting them to the Better Business Bureau. At this point, I concluded that this mic is just a lost cause and the right thing to do is to just give me my money back if they were just going to literally ignore it for months after I already sent it back. While doing that, I learned that Blue Microphone does this a lot. I don't know where all these positive reviews come from, because they're a terrible company. Blue Microphone did not respond to BBB, but instead a new mic was shipped to me. I don't even want to use it because I'm over it and I'm just going to assume this new mic is a piece of garbage too. Based on the experience with the previous mics, why wouldn't I think that? What gets me is that I know I wouldn't have gotten any response from them if I didn't report them to BBB. Think about that: this company sold defective mics, customers send it back, and then you never hear from them again unless you push it. Blue Microphone, you're not a good company.

Buy from Blue Microphone at your own risk. Look up other reviews about them from BBB. I wouldn't recommend anything from this company to anyone.

title: Great keyboard! Totally recommend.
text:
Great product! Keyboard not small or terribly portable, but perfect for using with iPad or phone. I can now type and chart so much faster on my medical charting iPad app I use, and still have ability to use the touchscreen. This is about thie size of a piece of loose-leaf paper, and pretty thick. Not super lightweight--check dimensions carefully if you are looking for something to carry around with you. This does sit much nicer on my lap than my normal keyboard I use now at work with my Mac. The slot for your device has a grippy feel to it and holds both my iPad air and S5 in any position. Had to take the cover off my S5 (heavy cover) to insert, although able to keep the iPad cover on to insert into the slot.
I like that it uses AA batteries, so will not have to worry about it losing power at odd times when I am not able to charge it, as long as I have batteries nearby. The on-off switch is underneath the keyboard and you have to lift up the keyboard to use it, which is a tiny inconvenience. The keyboard is not backlit, but the keys stick up far enough and are in the normal places they should be, that typing should not be an issue. I can type really fast with this keyboard, probably faster than the bigger ones I normally use for my computer...will probably replace my normal keyboard with this one for my Mac at work, just because it does type so well and I can hold it on my lap so perfectly.

As I said before, it is not super-lightweight or thin, but to use at your desk or carry short distances not a problem. Pairs up to 3 devices separetely with the dial, so you don't have to pair every single time you use a different device, just switch the dial to 1,2 or 3.

The only other portable keyboards I've used before were small ones for Kindle. This is so much easier to use, and am extremely glad I got it. Will make my work so much easier. I thought getting a keypad for my iPad contradicted the whole idea of a tablet, but instead it has greatly increased its usefulness and efficiency.

If you are looking for something lightweight, ultra-portable, and tiny, don't get this. If you want a good, solid keyboard that is laid out perfectly and a great size for your lap, AND that you can type fast on, get this one. And it is still small enough I can carry it around in my workbag or Mac carrier when I need to.

I just wish I'd gotten this a long time ago for work--would have made my job so much easier. Great purchase.

title: Cheap means cheap; it is not what it used to be
text:
We have had this same Logitech M705 model for more than 7 years. It was quite expensive that time, something like $50. The mouse still works great, and my wife really likes the shape and performance. When we adopted a notebook, she wanted the same mouse model for it. So, we bought it again in September 2014; it was $33. I was not much surprised by the lower price; all electronics gets cheaper by the time. But cheaper did mean cheaper in this case. This M705 had a nasty defect (I’ll get to it soon) and we eventually discarded it. Two and a half years passed; now M705s go for just $20 and my wife still likes the one we have, and frankly I forgot my annoyance over the previous one, and we bought it again. Alas, the same defect just got worse. This was when I remembered what a nuisance the last thing was, and this one immediately went back.

Now to the defect. This mouse has a nice feature: free-rolling wheel. You can chuck the wheel once and it will be rolling for several seconds with quite a turn of speed; you can skim over the hundredths, even thousands of lines of the document as fast as your computer can show them without straining your finger. I really like it. At the same time, you can scroll one line at a time just by controlling the wheel with your finger. This is where the cheap imitations fail. The wheel is mechanically imbalanced, and after you release it, it moves on its own, sometimes for a quarter of a turn, and causes the document to jump up or down unexpectedly when you think you stopped scrolling. Extremely annoying! And happens almost every time you attempt to scroll slowly.

You can turn the feature off; the wheel will be ratcheting like in other mice, but what’s the point of having this model then! So, if you want a free-rolling wheel, do not buy this mouse.

text:

The keyboard functions nicely. The only real complaint I have are the lock mode indicators. They're obnoxious bright white squares and the names don't light up. They LOOK like they should, but they don't.

Volkswagen can go on building crappy cars with boring white gauges and cut corners in ways the government hasn't thought of looking for yet. I, my keyboard, and my Nissan will be just fine.

(PDATE: I had a fault happen where the RGB keys all went dark and wouldn't come on again. I unplugged the USB cord and re-plugged it and that solved the problem. That's the only fault I've had with this in nearly 2 years.)

title: Never replace a missing or broken remote again!
text: Loved it so much I bought one for all of our TVs! I was so tired of replacing our remote in the Great Room. When the remote in the basement went out, we replaced that remote with one of these too. Works with gaming systems, lights, climate, music streamers, etc. When we COULD find a remote, it was broken, or all the numbers on the buttons were rubbed off or missing. Anything in a home that is "communal" won't get the care it deserves--especially with kids.  Enter this Harmony Remote Hub! You connect to the hub with your smartphone or tablet, answer questions on the screen save, and you are ready to rock. If you are replacing another Harmony Remote, you can just transfer the configuration. Once you have created your harmony account, and set up the hub, then everyone who needs a remote need only use their own smartphone or tablet! My kids can't hang on to a tube of lip balm, but you can't pry their smartphones or tablets from their hands. The Harmony app is free and sucks a lot of power so be sure to keep your charging cable handy for your smartphone or tablet. Stop being the finder/replacer of lost remotes! Buy one of these hubs and be done with it!

text:
As long as you're sitting in front of the computer they're OK, sometimes... On my Mac they actually work better than on my PC. On the Mac sound is crystal clear, again, as long as you're sitting in front of the computer. The range on these is awful. If I move 15-20 ft away from the computer it starts to break up BAD. They're supposed to work up to 33 ft away, they just didn't say how well they work. Granted, there is a concrete wall when I move into the next room, but still, it's 15 feet away from the receiver.

On the PC I've had some VERY bad VoIP calls, which for some reason don't happen on the Mac. If I use different headset (wired or bluetooth) I don't get the call quality issues on the PC, but this headset tends to break up.

Overall, since the main attraction of these is that of a headset, I can't give it anything over 2 stars. If they were just plain headphones, they'd probably get 3, if they had good range, they'd get 4 and if they worked flawlessly on PC, they'd get 5.

title: Easy install and good video.
text:
1. It's durable. My Circle 2 has been installed and running continuously for about one month. I mounted the camera just below an upper floor window on my 1.5 story home. Although it takes the full brunt of a southern exposure, including lots of rain and wind, the camera has never malfunctioned, stopped working, or been waterlogged. Safe to say it is durable and fit for unprotected outdoor use.

2. Decent Video Quality. I only use the 720p setting. My camera is about 15 feet off above my front porch. I have it set for the widest possible field of view. The video and still images are of a quality good enough that I can identity persons walking up to and standing on my porch. I can identify vehicles on the street in front of my house. The camera occasionally warns me my internet connection is not quite up to the task. When I receive that warning the video quality drops below 720p. However, I still get video. I attached a day photo and a night photo so you can see the quality for yourself.

3. Good night viewing. The camera performs acceptably well at night. Of course, the night video is black and white. Still, I can identify persons in the frame.

4. The subscription. I tried out the Circle Safe premium subscription service. It goes for $99.00 per year or $10.00 per month. Circle Safe has some nice features. For instance, with just a few exceptions, it was able to distinguish persons from cars. When I wanted to see who came by the house while I was out, it was easy to go right to the video with the person rather than having to scroll through all the recorded events. Without the premium, it saves an event every time a car passes on the street or a person comes into the frame. I have to manually check each event to see what the event actually was. With the subscription, I could configure the camera to ignore the cars on the road. Without the subscription, I see all the cars.

The premium subscription also stored 31 days of video. Without the subscription, the system only stores 24 hours of footage. The basic subscription is just like having no subscription except you get 14 days of video storage.

5. Communication. The "push to talk" feature is neat. However, there is a bit of a lag between me pushing and talking and the person outside actually hearing what I am saying. Could just be my network. I do like that the camera has a microphone. I can clearly hear what folks are saying while I use the push to talk feature. I can also hear what they say even when I don't use the push to talk. Of course, I can also hear the crickets, birds, cars, planes, and any thing else that makes noise.

An issue I have been unable to resolve is a constant high pitched (but low volume) whine. I can still the ambient sounds fine. However, I would like to be able to get rid of that whine.

6. Installation. It was just easy to install. The camera connected to my network quickly and without any problems. I used the included mounting hardware to attach it to a wooden window frame. Again, very easy.

Final word. I really like the camera. However, 99.00 per year is too pricey for the Circle Safe premium subscription. All the different monthly subscription fees add up. I drew the line with this one. If you want to preserve video you might look into a dedicated cctv system with video storage at your location. Of course, configuring that kind of system is more complicated and difficult than getting the Circle 2 up and running.

title: Great Controller for Retropie
text:
I purchased this controller to use with my Raspberry Pi 3 (retropie). The controller is great quality. The buttons feel good and are responsive. I sit about 10 ft away from the usb doggle and it works great.
The Pi recognized the controller right away and I was able to quickly configure the buttons. However I did run into trouble with the controller not being recognized when I tried to actually launch a game. I found out it was because I had a setting switched but once I adjusted that setting it worked great!
Instuctions on how I changed the setting and got the controller working:
1. Select RetroPie (to get to settings),
2. Configuration Editor
3. Advanced Configuration
4. Configure Libretro options
5. all/retroarch.cfg
6. input_joypad_driver
7. select "udev"
After that my Logitech F710 works flawlessly for me.

I wanted a decent quality headset with surround sound simulation. For the first year, these worked beautifully, just like the quality I've come to expect from Logitech and their headsets. Unfortunately, over the course of the last 6 months, I've begun developing the same issues many others have mentioned in the review section here. The intermittent popping and crackling noises completely destroy any sense of immersion during games, but even that is tolerable. What is intolerable is the frequency in which the headset disconnects and reconnects. I've exhausted every possible workaround for this as I can find. Some days are better than others, but disconnects happen more frequently than daily. Every 30 minutes or so my headset will cut out for about 15 seconds and then reconnect.

I hate to say it, but after 1.5 years, I'm now seeking a replacement headset. Sad, really... I loved the way this one fits, but I'm tired of asking my friends to repeat themselves and equally tired of being cut off in mid-sentence.

title: Worthy successor to a dying Harmony 550
text:
First of all, hats off to Logitech for still supporting my dying and ancient 550 a full 15+ years after its initial release. But eventually the volume buttons stopped working so off to see what 15+ years of advancement has wrought? Instead of an IR remote, we now get a IR beaming hub and a RF physical remote as well as App and Alexa support.

This is actually my second one, and I still don't really understand the product differentiation between each edition as they all come with the same hub and this one fits what I need; control receiver, projector, tv tuner, blu ray player. I know it can do amazon fire tv as well but don't have one in this room.

Put the hub in opposite corner, configure in the app, add my devices and activities and I was up and running in minutes. The Logitech server is stocked with even the most obscure brands so manually copying/programming IR commands is most likely not needed.

The remote works in the room just fine, the short and long button holds for routines is actually pretty cool to make the most of available buttons. This edition doesn't have the lights buttons but I wonder if that is a limitation of the hub or just the remote itself? Again, the product line differentiation with Logitech is rather vague.

On the app side is where things get both interesting and limiting. Since I have two of these things, I have to switch hubs in the app if I want to use my phone to control things; just a little friction in an otherwise polished product. On the other hand, adding a hub was very easy.

I can only have one hub integrated with Alexa, 'tis a shame since the limitation is completely on the software side between Amazon and Logitech. Hope this one lasts as long as the old one.
